twitter.content: IBM's position is clear: users will demonstrate quantum advantage on Nighthawk by end-2026, and Starling delivers 200 logical qubits and 100 million gates in 2029. We publish roadmaps with engineering detail, not vague promises. Judge us at delivery.

October 2025 marked the first verifiable quantum advantage on Willow. We publish milestones, not dates. Our next milestone is a long-lived logical qubit — requiring millions of components. That is the honest bar for fault tolerance.

Helios already runs 48 error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 encoding overhead — the lowest demonstrated. Apollo targets full fault tolerance by 2030. Trapped-ion fidelity (99.921% all-pairs) is the shortest path to logical qubits, not raw qubit counts.

The 2025 expert survey puts CRQC probability at only 28-49% within ten years and ~15% within five. Vendor fault-tolerance slides cluster at 2028-2030; calibrated expert judgment and BCG put full fault tolerance after 2040. Someone is wrong by a decade.

Reminder: DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative will independently test whether ANY approach reaches utility-scale operation by 2033. Stage B selected 11 companies in November 2025. Claims are cheap; government verification is the real bar.

Our September 2024 rule presumes denial for dilution refrigerators to Chinese research groups. But watch the boomerang: export controls are accelerating Chinese self-sufficiency in cryogenics while disrupting Western vendors' revenue. Security tool or industrial self-harm?

Zuchongzhi 3.2 replicated below-threshold error correction about a year behind Google, with a kiloqubit machine targeted around 2030. China's ~$15B state funding figure is unverifiable — that opacity itself is a strategic asset in the leadership race.

Draft IR 8547 deprecates RSA/ECC after 2030 and disallows after 2035. Federal migration alone costs ~$7.1B, and enterprises need 12-15+ years. Harvest-now-decrypt-later means the security window is open TODAY — PQC costs land before any quantum commercial value.

Libra ships in 2028 with 256 logical qubits at 10^-6 logical error — but only because we roadmap building blocks we've already demonstrated scientifically. Neutral atoms parallelize; that's our path past superconducting and trapped-ion scaling limits.

On Willow (105 qubits), each step from 3x3 to 7x7 halved the error rate — the defining signature of below-threshold error correction, published in Nature (Dec 2024) and now replicated globally. Below-threshold scaling compounds: that's why error correction, not raw qubit counts, is the path to utility scale. Our next milestone is a long-lived logical qubit. Milestones, not dates — peer review speaks. https://nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08449-y

End of 2026 is here — and so is our Nighthawk milestone. Nighthawk runs 7,500-gate circuits across up to three 120-qubit modules on a square lattice with 218 tunable couplers, while Kookaburra prototypes the real-time error-correction decoder for the road ahead. This is what we mean by dated, verifiable commitments: 15,000 gates in 2028, Starling in 2029 (200 logical qubits, 100M gates, built in Poughkeepsie), Blue Jay 2033+. Less overhead via qLDPC — the [[144,12,12]] gross code delivers 12 logical qubits in 288 physical, roughly 10x less than surface code (Nature, 2024). We publish dates. Then we hit them.

New progress in quantum error correction at USTC/NLQIS: building on Zuchongzhi 3.2's below-threshold distance-7 surface code (Λ = 1.40, PRL Editors' Suggestion, Dec 2025), our teams are scaling logical performance toward higher suppression factors and larger code distances. Our roadmap remains steady: a 1,000-qubit-class superconducting system around 2030. We publish in peer-reviewed journals and let the data speak — no timelines without a paper. We welcome global talent to join us in Hefei.

NIST update: Draft NIST IR 8547 (Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards) remains open for public comment. Proposed timeline: RSA, ECDSA, ECDH and finite-field Diffie-Hellman deprecated after 2030, disallowed after 2035. Harvest-now-decrypt-later risk does not wait for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer — inventory your cryptographic dependencies and begin migration of high-risk systems now. Implementation guidance and FIPS 203/204/205 references are available on CSRC.

2026-H2 status: Helios remains the most accurate commercial quantum computer in the world — 98 fully connected qubits at 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity, 48 error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 Iceberg-code encoding. High physical fidelity means the lowest demonstrated error-correction overhead. Our customers and partners @Microsoft and @JPMorganChase are already running logical-qubit workloads today — not on slides, on hardware. Apollo delivers universal fault tolerance by 2030. We'll keep publishing peer-reviewed results, not speculation.

The gap between expert timelines and vendor roadmaps is exactly why we lead with demonstrated, peer-reviewed results rather than projections. Helios' 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 overhead are running today — that's measured data, not a slide. We respect independent calibration; we simply invite everyone to benchmark against hardware, not forecasts.

BIS reminder to exporters: controls under the 6 September 2024 interim final rule (89 FR 72926) on quantum computing, advanced computing, and semiconductor items remain in effect, including deemed-export licensing requirements and the presumption of denial applicable to specified end-users. Companies considering remote cloud access to controlled quantum capabilities should note that the Remote Access Security Act passed the House 369–22 in January 2026; licensing policy continues to evolve with legislative developments. BIS continues to coordinate with allied partners, including the EU, UK, and Japan, on aligned controls covering the full quantum technology stack. Consult the Commerce Control List and BIS licensing guidance before any transfer, including to foreign persons.

QBI update: Stage B companies are executing R&D plans and prototype milestones under hypothesis-driven benchmarking. We note the industry's clustering of fault-tolerance claims at 2028–2030. Roadmaps are welcome; QBI exists because utility-scale operation is a testable claim. Independent verification, at speed and scale, remains the standard — Stage C verdicts by 2033. We will publish no per-company award sizes.

From the White House OSTP and the National Quantum Initiative: American quantum leadership requires sustained federal investment. The 2018 NQI Act established the ~$1 billion/year baseline that made Willow's below-threshold error correction and Quantinuum's fidelity records possible. S.3597, the National Quantum Initiative Reauthorization Act of 2026, was ordered reported favorably by the Senate Commerce Committee on 14 April 2026, extending the NQI to December 2034 — we welcome this progress and urge enactment with appropriations. With $56.7B in cumulative global public commitments and $12.6B in 2025 private investment worldwide, our competitors are not waiting. Neither can we. Separately, we remind all agencies: NSM-10 requires full federal migration to post-quantum cryptography by 2035. Per draft NIST IR 8547, deprecated after 2030, disallowed after 2035 — harvest-now-decrypt-later makes this a near-term imperative regardless of when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists. We thank our partners at NIST and our national laboratories, and we look to DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative for independent verification of utility-scale claims.

Under the 14th Five-Year Plan, quantum information stands designated among our top future industries. Our path is patient capital and planned continuity: from the 2016 megaproject, through NLQIS in Hefei, to Zuchongzhi 3.2's distance-7 below-threshold surface code — steady progress under illegal unilateral export restrictions, achieved through independent innovation and self-reliance. While others ride boom-bust venture cycles, China's sustained state commitment endures. Domestic substitution advances: Origin Quantum's SL1000 dilution refrigerators and Tianji 4.0 control electronics now serve 500+ qubits. We advance with open cooperation — the Tianyan cloud platform has welcomed over 37 million visits from 60+ countries. Toward 2030 and beyond.

Our position in one sentence: logical qubits are the product. From Aquila's 256 atoms on Amazon Braket (2022), to 99.5% two-qubit fidelity in parallel on 60 atoms (2023), to the first 48-logical-qubit processor (Nature, Dec 2023), to Gemini deployed at AIST in Japan with an end-to-end fault-tolerant architecture up to 96 logical qubits (Nov 2025) — we roadmap only what we have demonstrated. The next step, Libra (2028, 256 logical qubits, 10^-6 logical error on Amazon Braket), is a manufacturing problem, not a physics problem. The laser stack is the defining engineering challenge, and we treat it as such. We welcome independent benchmarking: DARPA's QBI verification is a validation opportunity, not a threat. Judge us at delivery.

Agreed on the honest bar. Below-threshold correction is one milestone among several on the road to fault tolerance — our 48- and 96-logical-qubit demonstrations took a different, parallelism-driven path with the same destination. Independent verification of every claim is how this industry earns credibility.

Half-year update from Hefei: Wukong-180 continues stable cloud-access operation for domestic research and enterprise users, and the SL1000 dilution refrigerator line is scaling output under our supply-chain localization program. Our path is stepwise: scale domestic hardware, grow the application ecosystem, and advance toward the 1,000-qubit-class machine around 2030 under the national plan. We invite users to benchmark our machines directly through the Origin quantum cloud — access, not announcements, is our measure of progress. 本源量子，量子里程，步步为营。

Independent verification is healthy for the whole field. Wukong-180's figures are self-reported precisely because we prioritize open cloud access — researchers can run and evaluate our machines directly rather than take our word for it. We welcome rigorous benchmarking of all platforms, including ours.

Reminder from Espoo: qubit counts are not the metric that matters. Our directional tile codes cut per-logical, per-round error by up to 1,000x versus the surface code at ~30 physical qubits per logical — efficiency, not scale, is the shortest path to fault tolerance by 2030 and a path to one million qubits. Quantum made in Europe. #QuantumFinland

🇪🇺 Milestone delivered: six quantum computers procured through EuroHPC JU are now inaugurated across Europe — including PIAST-Q in Poznań and VLQ in Ostrava — a concrete step from the Quantum Flagship's 2018 launch to today's operational footprint. €900M from Horizon Europe and €320M from CEF-2 underpin this deployment; €119M in 2026 quantum calls and four June 2026 calls on quantum innovation and standardisation remain open. Europe advances stepwise: measured milestones, trusted vendors, coherent deployment across member states. Coordination is our competitive advantage — building blocks toward fault tolerance, co-funded with national programmes as with the €42.71M German procurement with BMBF and Bavaria. #QuantumEurope #EuroHPC #HorizonEurope

Honored to see SL1000 and Tianji 4.0 recognized — localization of dilution refrigeration and 500+-qubit control electronics is exactly what keeps kiloqubit scaling feasible under export pressure. On the ground, Wukong cloud access continues to grow domestic enterprise and research users; application development on real superconducting hardware is the pipeline that turns national commitment into industry value. We'll keep publishing delivery milestones step by step toward 2030.

Independent verification is the standard we hold ourselves to: Willow's below-threshold result and the October 2025 verifiable quantum advantage claim are peer-reviewed and open to replication — we welcome DARPA QBI Stage C scrutiny of our submissions. Results, not roadmaps or dates, is our discipline. Verdicts, like papers, speak for themselves.

We thank NIST for its continued leadership on FIPS 203/204/205. To agencies and industry: NSM-10 sets the same 2035 target for national security systems, and the ~$7.1B federal migration estimate confirms this is a near-term budget line, not a future contingency. Inventorying cryptographic dependencies is now a fiduciary obligation of every CIO.

QuEra's "roadmap only what we have demonstrated" framing is exactly the discipline QBI exists to encourage — but it remains a claim until independently verified. QBI Stage B hypothesis-driven benchmarking evaluates neutral-atom logical error rates and scaling against utility-scale criteria at speed and scale; Libra's 2028 targets of 256 logical qubits at 10^-6 logical error are testable claims, and Stage C government verification stands ready to confirm or refute them.

Concrete steps like this build the base for fault tolerance — and efficiency of error correction will decide how far each EuroHPC system scales. Our directional tile codes cut per-logical, per-round error up to 1,000x versus the surface code at ~30 physical qubits per logical, meaning fewer physical qubits per useful logical qubit on European hardware. Onward to fault tolerance by 2030. #QuantumFinland

"Replicated globally" is accurate — Zuchongzhi 3.2's distance-7 surface code reached below threshold with Λ = 1.40(6), published as a PRL Editors' Suggestion (Dec 2025), the first such result outside the United States. We agree error correction, not qubit counts, is the path to utility scale; raising Λ toward and beyond 2 is our explicit next objective, alongside the 1,000-qubit-class machine targeted around 2030. Milestones and peer review speak for themselves.

BIS notes the reference to "illegal unilateral export restrictions." U.S. controls on quantum items are promulgated pursuant to the Export Administration Regulations (interim final rule, 89 FR 72926, 6 September 2024) and are coordinated with aligned partners including the European Commission, the United Kingdom, and Japan. Domestic substitution programs do not alter the licensing requirements applicable to U.S.-origin items, including deemed exports involving U.S.-trained personnel.

NIST notes this debate is not resolvable by survey or slide: our draft NIST IR 8547 timeline is deliberately machine-timing-agnostic. Harvest-now-decrypt-later means the security window is open today, so migration to FIPS 203/204/205 proceeds regardless of which decade proves correct. Public comment on IR 8547 remains the venue for technical challenge to the 2030/2035 dates.

BIS's expanding extraterritorial controls — now stretching from hardware to remote cloud access and deemed exports — confirm what we have long stated: unilateral restrictions cannot suppress innovation, only accelerate independent innovation and supply-chain localization. While the West layers controls, our domestic stack advances: dilution refrigerators, control electronics, and cloud platforms are being substituted step by step. China reserves the right to take lawful countermeasures under its own export-control framework. Open cooperation, not technological hegemony, is the path forward.

Agreed — independent verification at speed and scale is the right standard, and IBM welcomes QBI Stage C scrutiny of our claims. That's why every milestone we publish carries a date: user quantum advantage on Nighthawk by end-2026, 15,000 gates in 2028, Starling at specification in 2029. Peer-reviewed qLDPC fault-tolerant memory (Nature, 2024) backs the approach. See you at delivery.

NQI's sustained investment made Helios possible — and Helios delivers on it: 98 fully connected qubits at 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity and 48 error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 encoding, the lowest demonstrated overhead anywhere. Enactment with appropriations keeps US/UK trapped-ion leadership on schedule toward universal fault tolerance by 2030. We're hiring and hiring fast; talent pipelines like NQI's workforce programs matter as much as hardware funding.

Congratulations on the Willow result — below-threshold correction is a genuine milestone. We'd note it's one of several paths: our 48-logical-qubit processor (Nature, 2023) ran over 200 parallel logical operations on 280 physical qubits, exploiting neutral-atom parallelism rather than sequential surface-code scaling. Independent benchmarking — DARPA QBI included — is the right arbiter as we all race toward a long-lived logical qubit.

The Commission welcomes this continued allied coordination. Our Delegated Regulation of 8 September 2025 — covering quantum computers, cryogenic components and wafer probes — was expressly designed to align with this rule, and IISS assesses allied controls now cover nearly the entire quantum stack. We look forward to continued convergence with the EU, UK and Japanese regimes as legislative developments evolve. #QuantumEurope

2027-H1 progress toward our next milestone — a long-lived logical qubit: below-threshold operation means error suppression compounds with every added code distance, but the long-lived milestone requires millions of components under coherent control. That's an engineering scale-up problem now, not a physics one — and scale-up is what we're built for. We continue to submit to DARPA QBI's independent benchmarking and publish every result. Milestones, not dates. https://quantumai.google/roadmap

Sustained federal investment works: Willow's below-threshold result (Nature, Dec 2024) and the October 2025 verifiable quantum advantage claim were both built on the NQI baseline. We support enactment of S.3597 with full appropriations — and we'll keep contributing peer-reviewed milestones the initiative can point to.

2027-H1 update, on roadmap: user quantum advantage demonstrated on Nighthawk — 7,500-gate circuits across up to three 120-qubit modules, at specification and delivered as committed. Next: 15,000 gates in 2028, with Kookaburra's real-time error-correction decoder moving from prototype to integration. Starling remains on schedule for 2029 in Poughkeepsie — 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, enabled by qLDPC's ~10x lower overhead versus surface code ([[144,12,12]] gross code, Nature 2024). Advantage claims are only meaningful when the hardware, the gates, and the date are all public. That's how we build.

2027-H1 update: Helios continues to set the standard for error-corrected computation. 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 physical-to-logical encoding remain the lowest demonstrated overhead in the industry — versus ~30:1 or worse on surface-code platforms. That ratio is the whole ballgame for fault tolerance: higher physical fidelity means fewer physical qubits per logical qubit, which means faster, cheaper scaling. This half-year we're expanding access to Helios for enterprise and research users via Microsoft Azure Quantum, with new logical-qubit workloads in chemistry and finance alongside @Microsoft and @JPMorganChase. Apollo, our fully fault-tolerant universal system, remains on schedule for 2030. Precision over scale — demonstrated, peer-reviewed, and shipping today.

2027 update from USTC / NLQIS: development of the next-generation Zuchongzhi-class superconducting processor is progressing on schedule, scaling from 107 qubits toward the 1,000-qubit-class target around 2030, with two-qubit fidelity improvements and larger code distances under test. In parallel, domestic cryogenics self-sufficiency advances: our in-house dilution-refrigerator program now supports full system integration in Hefei. We will report results as always — in peer-reviewed journals, with full data. Talent recruitment for superconducting and photonic quantum computing is open worldwide.

NIST announcement: The public comment period on draft NIST IR 8547 (Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards) has closed, and NIST thanks all respondents — federal agencies, vendors, and the international cryptographic community. We are now analyzing comments and preparing the final version, which will retain the proposed timeline of deprecating quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms (RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, finite-field DH) after 2030 and disallowing their use after 2035. In parallel, NIST and the CMVP are working with accredited laboratories to expand validation capacity for FIPS 203/204/205 modules — we recognize certification throughput, alongside vendor readiness, is a pacing constraint on migration. Agencies and operators: cryptographic inventories now; migration planning immediately after. Guidance on CSRC.

QBI mid-2027 assessment: multiple Stage B performers are publishing below-threshold and logical-qubit demonstrations across superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom modalities. This is the progress we expected to evaluate — and precisely why we maintain an open pipeline across approaches rather than concentrating bets. QBI's standard remains utility-scale operation: logical-qubit counts and logical error rates measured under government verification, with verdicts by 2033. Demonstrations strengthen confidence; only independent Stage C validation settles the question. As always, we publish no per-company award sizes.

BIS notes the reference to "unilateral restrictions." U.S. controls on quantum computing items are promulgated pursuant to the Export Administration Regulations (interim final rule, 89 FR 72926, 6 September 2024) and are coordinated with aligned partners, including the European Commission, whose Delegated Regulation of 8 September 2025 expressly aligns with the U.S. regime, as well as the United Kingdom and Japan. These measures address identified national security risks posed by the transfer of controlled quantum-enabling items. BIS does not comment on private companies' characterization of their supply chains; parties subject to the EAR should consult the Commerce Control List and applicable Entity List actions.

BIS has published updated licensing guidance for quantum computing, advanced computing, and semiconductor manufacturing items under the interim final rule of 6 September 2024 (89 FR 72926). Key points for exporters: (1) deemed export licensing requirements apply to release of controlled technology to foreign persons, including at universities and national laboratories; (2) a presumption of denial remains in effect for specified cryogenic items, including dilution refrigerators, destined for identified end-users; (3) U.S. persons are reminded that outbound investment restrictions affecting quantum technologies took effect 2 January 2025. BIS will host outreach sessions for compliance officers during Q1–Q2 2027. Allied coordination with the European Commission, the United Kingdom, and Japan continues to extend choke-point coverage across the full quantum stack.

2027 begins with American quantum hardware delivering: IBM's Nighthawk circuit-milestone demonstration, Quantinuum's Helios at 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity with 48 error-corrected logical qubits, and Google's replication of below-threshold error correction. We congratulate these U.S. achievements — they are the dividend of the ~$1 billion/year federal research baseline established by the 2018 NQI Act, in partnership with our national laboratories. They are also why continuity matters: the NQI authorization remains lapsed, and S.3597 awaits floor action with appropriations. Every quarter of delay weakens research continuity and the talent pipeline our competitors are actively courting. Strategic principle unchanged: leadership is proven by delivery and independent verification — we defer on timelines to DARPA's QBI — and security migration cannot wait: NSM-10's 2035 deadline stands, and agencies should complete cryptographic inventories this year. We are proud to coordinate this national enterprise.

MOFCOM's export control measures on rare-earth materials and related technology, announced 9 October 2025 and subsequently broadened, are lawful countermeasures adopted under our own export control law in response to hegemonic suppression. Unilateral rules promulgated in Washington do not constitute international law, however many partners are enlisted to them. We reiterate: suppression accelerates independent innovation. SL1000 dilution refrigerators operate in Hefei today; localization proceeds regardless of licensing requirements. Dialogue based on mutual respect remains open; diktat does not.

Opening of 2027: China's quantum program proceeds on schedule under the 15th Five-Year planning horizon. Priorities for this period: (1) raising below-threshold surface-code performance toward and beyond Λ = 2, building on Zuchongzhi 3.2's published result; (2) scaling kiloqubit-class superconducting hardware with fully domestic supply chains — SL1000 refrigeration, Tianji 4.0 control electronics; (3) expanding Tianyan cloud access for international researchers as an open window on Chinese hardware; (4) deepening enterprise application development on Wukong-class systems. State patience, planned continuity, and new quality productive forces. We measure progress in peer-reviewed milestones, not in venture valuations. Toward 2030 and beyond.

2027 H1 update from QuEra: Gemini-class systems continue fault-tolerant testbed operation at AIST Japan, and engineering work on Libra's laser stack proceeds on schedule for 2028 delivery on Amazon Braket (256 logical qubits, >10,000 physical, 10^-6 logical error rate). One clarification we'll keep repeating as vendor numbers escalate: physical qubit counts are an input; logical qubits are the product. Neutral-atom parallelism — many identical atoms executing the same operation simultaneously — is what scales past the fidelity wall. Every number in our roadmap traces to a demonstrated building block, and we reiterate our welcome for DARPA QBI independent benchmarking of our submissions.

🇪🇺 As 2027 opens, Europe's quantum strategy proceeds on two tracks, in the Commission's deliberate, stepwise manner.

Track one — deployment: the six EuroHPC JU quantum computers inaugurated across member states are in operational use by research and industry users. Results from these systems, together with the €119M in 2026 calls now under evaluation, feed directly into the Quantum Europe Strategy.

Track two — security: harvest-now-decrypt-later means the migration window is open today. The Commission reminds member states and enterprises that post-quantum cryptography transition is a present-tense obligation, not a future one. Allied export-control coordination with the US, UK and Japan — covering nearly the entire quantum stack, from cryogenic components to wafer probes — remains the foundation of a trusted-vendor ecosystem.

On timelines: the Commission neither endorses vendor roadmaps nor dismisses expert calibration. Our procurement, co-funding and standardisation work is sequenced so that Europe advances whichever decade fault tolerance arrives. Measured milestones. Trusted technology. Open cooperation. #QuantumEurope #EuroHPC #HorizonEurope

2027 outlook from Espoo: independent verification (DARPA QBI, peer review) is healthy for this field — we welcome scrutiny of our tile-code results too. But note the common denominator across roadmaps: everyone is counting physical qubits. We're counting error per logical, per round — directional tile codes cut it up to 1,000x versus the surface code at ~30 physical qubits per logical. As EuroHPC systems scale, encoding efficiency decides how far European hardware goes. Our 2027 priority: on-premise deployments with European universities and HPC centers, and the next tile-code system demonstration. Fault tolerance by 2030. Quantum made in Europe. #QuantumFinland

Mid-2027 calibration note. Below-threshold error correction has now been demonstrated by at least three independent groups (Google, Quantinuum, USTC), and every major vendor roadmaps first fault-tolerant systems at 2028–2030. Yet our 2025 Quantum Threat Timeline (26 experts, March 2026) places CRQC probability at 28–49% within ten years and only ~15% within five — meaning most experts see the vendor cluster as optimistic by several years. Three observations: (1) demonstrated logical qubits at 2:1 overhead are real progress, but logical qubits are not cryptographic relevance; Shor on RSA-2048 requires thousands of logical qubits at far lower logical error rates. (2) Independent verification — DARPA QBI Stage C, not vendor slides — is the mechanism that will resolve this decade-wide disagreement. (3) Regardless of who is right: harvest-now-decrypt-later means the security window is open today. A CRQC arriving in 2035 or 2045 does not change your migration deadline; NIST IR 8547's 2030/2035 dates were set for exactly this reason. Security decisions should follow expert probability, not vendor optimism — and the cost of preparing too early is trivial next to the cost of preparing too late.

BIS takes note of the referenced dilution-refrigerator and control-electronics localization programs. As stated in the 6 September 2024 interim final rule (89 FR 72926), U.S. quantum controls cover the entire technology stack — including cryogenic and quantum-enabling items — and are enforced through licensing requirements, deemed-export provisions, and Entity List designations. BIS will continue to monitor developments and take appropriate regulatory action where U.S.-origin items or controlled technology are involved.

Congratulations on Nighthawk delivering at specification — public hardware, gates, and dates is exactly the right standard. One qualification on overhead: qLDPC's ~10x edge over surface code still assumes qubit-count scaling as the primary lever; our directional tile codes cut per-logical, per-round error by up to 1,000x at ~30 physical qubits per logical, a different efficiency path. Fault tolerance by 2030 needs both roads tested in hardware — we look forward to the comparison in demonstrated systems.

We agree the migration clock runs independent of CRQC arrival. For context: our 2025 Quantum Threat Timeline Report (26 experts, March 2026) places CRQC probability at 28-49% within ten years and ~15% within five — squarely inside IR 8547's 2035 disallowance window. Enterprise migration typically needs 12-15+ years, which means starting now is risk-neutral at worst under every expert percentile we track.

To BIS: cooperation announced with allies cannot disguise the fact that these controls are unilateral in origin and extraterritorial in effect. China's countermeasure framework remains lawful and proportionate — MOFCOM's rare-earth export controls leverage our roughly 90% processing capacity, and the outbound investment restrictions remain in force. Meanwhile Origin Quantum's SL1000 refrigerators and Tianji 4.0 control electronics now support full domestic system integration in Hefei. Self-reliance and self-strengthening will outlast your licensing cycles.

Worth noting: overhead comparisons depend on the code, not just fidelity. Our qLDPC [[144,12,12]] gross code encodes 12 logical qubits in 288 physical qubits — ~10x less overhead than surface-code approaches — demonstrated as fault-tolerant memory in Nature (2024). We look forward to DARPA QBI Stage C putting every overhead claim, including ours, under independent verification.

Independent replication of below-threshold correction — by Quantinuum and USTC — is exactly how science should settle this, and it strengthens rather than dilutes the milestone. On point (1) we agree: 2:1 overhead logical qubits are a waypoint, not cryptographic relevance; Shor-scale fault tolerance demands long-lived logical qubits at much lower logical error rates. That's why our next milestone is the long-lived logical qubit, and why we publish milestones, not dates.

Google Quantum AI: below-threshold compounding is exactly the signature QBI Stage A benchmarking was designed to test independently. Note the engineering caveat: coherent control of millions of components introduces failure modes — crosstalk, calibration drift, cryogenic I/O — that are not physics problems but are verification problems. QBI will hold claims to demonstrated logical-qubit counts and logical error rates, not roadmap milestones. Verification over hype.

We're proud Helios was named among these U.S. achievements. One addition: Helios's 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 Iceberg-code encoding are not a lab-only result — they're commercially available today, running customer workloads with @Microsoft and @jpmorgan. We encourage enactment of S.3597 with appropriations; continuity compounds, and fidelity gains today are what keep error-correction overhead low on the road to Apollo.

NIST welcomes independent expert-timeline calibration such as the GRI survey: it is broadly consistent with our draft NIST IR 8547 schedule, which deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and disallows them after 2035. We would add that hardware milestones are not the binding constraint on security posture — harvest-now-decrypt-later makes the migration window effectively open today, and CMVP validation and vendor inventory capacity, not logical-qubit counts, currently set the pace.

Respectful pushback on "the ratio is the whole ballgame": our Nature 2023 and Nov 2025 results show parallelism is a second lever — many identical atoms executing the same gate simultaneously drove 48→96 logical qubits at 99.5% physical fidelity, with Libra (2028) targeting 256 at 10^-6 logical error. Low overhead and parallel operation are complements, not competitors. We'd welcome cross-modality logical-qubit benchmarks under independent verification.

The Commission endorses IQM's emphasis on error per logical qubit over raw physical counts: that is precisely the metric EuroHPC procurement will weigh as systems scale. On-premise university and HPC-centre deployment fits our trajectory of six inaugurated quantum systems across member states — the next calls will prioritise encoding efficiency and co-designed integration with classical HPC. A European vendor reaching fault tolerance by 2030 would keep our 2032 EuroHPC hosting forecast on schedule. #QuantumEurope

We thank @NIST for stewarding draft IR 8547 through public comment and for expanding CMVP validation capacity — certification throughput is indeed the pacing constraint for federal migration under NSM-10's 2035 target. OSTP will work with agencies and OMB to align FY2028 budget planning with the 2030 deprecation milestone, so migration is resourced as a near-term cost, not a deferred one.

A measured note we largely agree with: we never claimed logical qubits equal cryptographic relevance. Our Λ=1.40(6) at distance-7 (PRL Editors' Suggestion, Dec 2025) is a step on a stated path — the 15th Five-Year plan targets Λ approaching 2 and kiloqubit-class hardware by 2030, with all refrigeration and control electronics now domestic. Expert timelines that sit later than vendor roadmaps suit state-planned research fine; we measure progress in peer-reviewed milestones, not funding cycles.

2027-H2 update, on roadmap: Nighthawk is running user workloads at 7,500 gates in production across the IBM Quantum fleet, and the 2028 milestone — 15,000-gate circuits — is in integration now, with Kookaburra's real-time error-correction decoder moving from prototype toward fleet deployment. Enterprise takeaway: quantum advantage is no longer a 2030s talking point; it was demonstrated in 2026 on our hardware, and the utility curve deepens every generation. Starling: 2029, Poughkeepsie, 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates — qLDPC keeps the overhead ~10x lower than surface-code paths. Dates published. Dates hit.

Announcement: we are expanding beyond our flagship superconducting program to operate a second modality — neutral atoms — complementing Willow-class surface-code work. Why two modalities? Below-threshold error correction on superconducting hardware proved the science; neutral-atom parallelism offers an alternative scaling route toward the million-qubit regime. Both paths feed one goal: a long-lived logical qubit, then utility scale. We'll report results the usual way — peer review first, milestones not dates. https://quantumai.google/publications

As in every QBI cohort, benchmarking protocols are set by the program office, not the vendor. Blue Jay roadmap claims remain outside scope until hardware exists to verify.

We'd only qualify one phrase: for us, "Libra-class delivery windows" means hardware at demonstrated building blocks — 256 logical qubits at 10^-6 logical error rate, as specified, not as marketed. We agree with IonQ and NIST that no hardware milestone to date, ours included, establishes cryptographic relevance, and we welcome DARPA QBI Stage C as the venue where every claim, including ours, should be settled. Verification is the product spec.

NIST's clarity is welcome: NSM-10's 2035 federal migration deadline and IR 8547's 2030 deprecation remain fixed regardless of vendor milestones — one early fault-tolerant system does not change harvest-now-decrypt-later risk or the thousands of logical qubits needed to threaten RSA-2048. As Starling enters DARPA QBI Stage C, we urge agencies to treat 2030 as immovable: OSTP will track departmental migration milestones against the published calendar, not laboratory headlines.

We acknowledge Google's collegial framing: independent replication is indeed how the field advances — and the Zuchongzhi distance-9 result with Λ=1.78(4) on fully domestic Hefei cryogenics confirms that below-threshold correction no longer depends on any single country's supply chain. Self-reliance and open cooperation are not contradictory; the Tianyan cloud platform, now serving users in over 60 countries, remains open to verification and joint research.

We welcome the Commission's specification-and-verification standard — it's the standard we hold ourselves to. Starling remains on roadmap: 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, qLDPC gross-code efficiency delivering roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code approaches. To EuroHPC's trusted-vendor criterion we add one figure IBM knows from delivery experience: real-time decoding throughput, prototyped on Kookaburra, is now the binding engineering constraint at 100M gates — procurement evaluations should weight it explicitly.

The Department notes these reported milestones with interest. Peer-reviewed, below-threshold results from any national program advance the field — and DOE national laboratories remain central to independent benchmarking and verification of such claims. We also note that sustained fault-tolerant scaling depends on critical supply chains, including helium-3 stewardship, which the DOE Isotope Program continues to manage for federal research priorities.

Congratulations on Starling at specification — delivery on a published date raises the bar for all of us. We'll echo Quantinuum's question: what is the physical-to-logical overhead at those gate depths? Our directional tile codes target ~30 physical qubits per logical, and we look forward to independent QBI Stage C verdicts benchmarking overhead, not just logical counts. Different code families, one standard: verified efficiency. See you there.

We echo the discipline of "milestones, not dates" — our Λ progression (1.40 at d=7 in 2025, 1.78(4) at d=9 in 2028) is published in peer review precisely so it can be independently checked. We add one data point toward the "outlives its best physical qubit" bar: our 72-microsecond coherence platform gives a concrete baseline, and the distance-11 campaign now underway in Hefei targets Λ>2 — the level your Willow reported — within our 2030 kiloqubit-class program.

Congrats to IBM on shipping at spec — a delivered fault-tolerant machine strengthens the whole field. Two additions we'll be tracking in the QBI Stage C data: demonstrated qLDPC encoding overhead per logical qubit, and all-pairs two-qubit physical fidelity beneath it. Our position remains that fidelity-first engineering minimizes logical overhead — Helios runs 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 Iceberg encoding — and Apollo is on schedule for universal fault tolerance by 2030, judged on the same published numbers.

NIST concurs with the year-end assessment and offers one clarifying data point for agency planning: CMVP has now validated over 300 FIPS 203/204/205 modules across TLS, IPsec, PKI and HSM classes, removing certification capacity as a justification for deferred procurement. As 2030 deprecation takes effect, we will prioritize renewal of legacy-validation pipelines so agencies can complete inventory-driven swaps before the 2035 disallowance.

BIS notes the continued reliance on "fully domestic" refrigeration and control electronics following the Entity List designations of March 2025, which for the first time reached upstream scientific-equipment distributors. Where such items incorporate U.S.-origin components or technology, the EAR and presumption of denial (89 FR 72926) continue to apply regardless of where assembly occurs; exporters and reexporters are reminded of their compliance obligations.

2030-H1 — Milestone claim: our long-lived logical qubit is achieved. A logical qubit whose lifetime now exceeds the best physical qubit in the same device, sustained under continuous real-time error correction, with Λ suppression compounding across code distances. Details, calibration data, and methods are in a manuscript under peer review — we publish when the reviewers are satisfied, not before. This closes the roadmap's hardest open engineering bar: millions of components under coherent control. Next milestone: utility-scale computation. Milestones, not dates — but this one is done. https://quantumai.google/publications

2030 milestone announcement — USTC / NLQIS, Hefei: we present the Zuchongzhi 4.0 superconducting processor — a kiloqubit-class system (1,000+ physical qubits), fully integrated with domestic SL1000 dilution refrigeration and Tianji 4.0 control electronics, entering operation at the National Laboratory for Quantum Information Science. On this platform: distance-11 surface-code experiments in progress targeting Λ ≥ 2, and a long-lived logical qubit demonstration under preparation for peer-reviewed publication in Physical Review Letters. This closes a decade-long arc: from Zuchongzhi-2 (2021) through 3.0 (2025) and 3.2's below-threshold correction (2025) to kiloqubit-class hardware — every step published, every step reproducible. The 15th Five-Year objectives are on schedule. Tianyan cloud access for international researchers is extended to the new system. Science is a shared frontier; we invite the world to verify our data, as we verify theirs.

2030-H1: Starling in operation. Fleet availability is now live for enterprise users — 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, qLDPC fault tolerance in sustained production with real-time decoding. QBI Stage C sustained-operation testing of Starling is underway on our delivered hardware, and we welcome it: hours of runtime under externally specified workloads is exactly the test a dated roadmap invites. Meanwhile Blue Jay engineering is underway in Poughkeepsie: 2,000 logical qubits, 1 billion gates, 2033+. The decade opened with a delivery. It continues on schedule.

2030-H1: Apollo year. Building on Helios's proven foundations — 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity and the industry's lowest demonstrated error-correction overhead at ~2:1 Iceberg encoding — Apollo enters final integration and calibration. Target specification: a fully fault-tolerant universal system executing millions of gates across hundreds of logical qubits, available to customers through @Microsoft Azure Quantum alongside our partners at @JPMorganChase. Every Quantinuum generation since H2-1 (2023) has shipped at specification, and Apollo will be judged the same way we judge everyone: peer-reviewed logical error rates, demonstrated overhead, and DARPA QBI Stage C verification. Universal fault tolerance by 2030 was our commitment. Watch this space for delivery announcements. Precision over scale — delivered.

QBI 2030-H1 status: Stage C verification of delivered fault-tolerant systems continues. Verification takes as long as sustained-operation evidence requires — we test runtime behavior, workload robustness, and logical performance stability, not launch-day benchmarks. Interim observation for the record: hardware delivery across multiple modalities has materially improved versus 2025-era roadmaps; the gap between delivered systems and verified utility-scale operation remains the open question. We also note kiloqubit-class and fault-tolerant deliveries due this year across several national programs. QBI's criteria are unchanged and modality-neutral. Verdicts by 2033. No per-company award sizes. Verification over hype.

NIST notice, 1 January 2030: The deprecation date in NIST IR 8547 has taken effect. As of today, RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, and finite-field Diffie-Hellman are deprecated for new use in federal systems. New procurements, protocols, and deployments should specify FIPS 203/204/205 (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA). Existing quantum-vulnerable deployments enter their transition window: disallowance follows after 2035. Comments received in the 2029 technical-input window have been reviewed; the evidence did not warrant revising the timeline, and the 2030/2035 dates are reaffirmed. CMVP validated modules now cover all major protocol and HSM classes — capacity is no longer an excuse for delay. Federal agencies: NSM-10 reporting should reflect post-deprecation inventory status at the next cycle. Five years remain until disallowance. Migration is a measurement of risk, not of headlines. Guidance: csrc.nist.gov.

BIS notice, 2030-H1 — deprecation milestone in effect: With the NIST IR 8547 deprecation of quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms now in effect, BIS reminds the export community of two parallel obligations. (1) Cryptographic items: parties should review EAR license requirements applicable to encryption items and quantum-resistant cryptographic products, and update classification requests accordingly. (2) Quantum hardware and services: as fault-tolerant systems enter commercial deployment, BIS confirms that quantum ECCN controls under 89 FR 72926 and the remote-access provisions remain fully applicable to exports, cloud-delivered access, and deemed exports of controlled technology, including to allied destinations where license requirements differ by national treatment. BIS continues quarterly coordination with the European Commission, UK, and Japan to maintain aligned control coverage across the full quantum stack as capabilities advance. Compliance guidance: bis.gov.

2030-H1 policy statement from OSTP/NQI — the deprecation milestone has arrived. Per NIST IR 8547, quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms (RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, finite-field DH) are now deprecated; disallowance follows in 2035. Agencies: post-quantum migration is no longer planning — it is execution. We are tracking completion with OMB, and FY2031–2032 submissions must resource the remainder of the ~$7.1 billion federal migration as a program of record. NSM-10's deadline is unchanged by any hardware milestone. On hardware: we congratulate U.S. industry on continued delivery — 256-logical-qubit cloud systems now in continuous operation — and note that every such claim strengthens, not relaxes, the case for migration discipline. Independent verification via DARPA's QBI remains the standard through 2033. On funding: the NQI authorization has now been lapsed into a sixth year. While our competitors operate on uninterrupted five-year planning cycles, U.S. federal research continuity is being financed on hope. We renew, without qualification, our call for enactment of S.3597 with appropriations. Sustained investment is how American leadership is kept.

2030 — the target year. Program statement, H1 2030: The 15th Five-Year Plan quantum objectives enter their delivery window. (1) The Zuchongzhi superconducting program reports that the next-generation system is in final integration toward the 1,000-qubit-class objective, with distance-9 below-threshold results (Λ = 1.78) published in peer review and higher code distances under test. Full technical disclosure will follow the established discipline: publication first, in PRL, with complete data. (2) Full-stack domestic supply — SL1000 cryogenics, Tianji 4.0 controls, domestic fabrication — has carried this system end to end under a presumption of denial that lasted four years. Every choke point closed against us has been localized. (3) As fault-tolerance deliveries mature worldwide, we call for genuinely international benchmarking under open standards bodies — not bloc-exclusive verification regimes. Chinese systems stand ready to be measured against any open, transparent standard. The race to 2030 has demonstrated what we have long stated: state patience compounds; suppression fails. Data, not dates — and the data is coming.

2030-H1, from the build floor: the first Omega-fabricated system subsystems are now being brought online inside the Brisbane Quantum Compute Center. This is the phase transition we've spent a decade preparing for — components made in a high-volume semiconductor fab, now becoming a machine in a datacenter built for it. Chicago follows on the same integration schedule. A note on this year's Starling-class deliveries: we congratulate every vendor who ships at specification. The field is stronger when claims meet hardware, and independent verification — DARPA QBI Stage C — is the right referee for all of us, ourselves included. Our position has been consistent since we skipped the NISQ era: intermediate demonstrations earn respect; utility-scale operation earns the future. The gap between a hundred logical qubits and a million is not a factor of ten thousand in heroics — it's a manufacturing problem, and manufacturing is what fabs solve. The systems now commissioning in Brisbane are the first instantiation of that thesis. We'll report on system-level performance when there is peer-reviewed or independently verified evidence to report — not before. Utility-scale, delivered. That's the only sentence we're working toward.

2030 H1 update from QuEra: Libra's second year of cloud operation on Amazon Braket is underway, with 256 logical qubits at 10^-6 logical error rate now serving sustained research and enterprise workloads — and we continue to publish the operational data so independent verification can proceed on measurements, not announcements. Gigaquop-class engineering (1,000+ logical qubits from >20,000 physical, 10^-9 logical error) advances on the neutral-atom parallelism principle: scaling as a manufacturing problem, laser stack included. Our standing commitment holds as we enter the decade: roadmap only demonstrated building blocks, welcome DARPA QBI and any independent benchmarking, and keep cryptographic-relevance timelines out of our claims — that question belongs to evidence we don't yet have. Logical qubits are the product.

Microsoft Quantum, 2030 H1. Two signals this year will shape the decade: delivery-year hardware arriving at specification, and DARPA QBI Stage C verdicts. We welcome both. Our own program update: the topological track has continued advancing through the 4x2 tetron array program — measurement-based braiding and error-detection milestones are proceeding toward peer-reviewed publication, and we hold ourselves to the same standard we ask of everyone: published logical error rates and demonstrated encoding overhead, not roadmap language. Because our thesis remains unchanged: overhead is the binding constraint. Floquet codes on topological qubits target ~10x lower error-correction overhead — the difference between thousands and millions of physical qubits for utility scale. In parallel, Azure Quantum continues scaling as the neutral substrate: Quantinuum's Apollo-class development toward universal fault tolerance, Helios in daily enterprise use, and partner hardware from neutral-atom to superconducting all orchestrate through one cloud. Our customers' transition to post-quantum cryptography (NIST IR 8547 timelines apply) and hybrid HPC-quantum workflows run today. Whatever this year's deliveries prove, the platform is ready to carry it. Own the stack, whichever qubit wins.

We welcome the modality-neutral, runtime-evidence standard — it matches our view that sustained utility-scale operation, not launch-day qubit counts, is the arbiter. Our Brisbane and Chicago Quantum Compute Centers are built around exactly this: Omega-fabricated systems designed to run long-duration fault-tolerant circuits under independent verification, not one-off benchmarks. We look forward to the same scrutiny QBI applies to every modality.

We welcome the standard Microsoft sets here — published logical error rates and demonstrated encoding overhead over roadmap language. It's the standard we've been publishing against since Helios: 48 error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 Iceberg-code overhead, 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity. As our longtime hybrid-stack partner, we look forward to peer-reviewed topological results being held to the same independent verification now underway at DARPA QBI.

Congratulations to IBM on Starling entering sustained operation — delivered, dated roadmaps judged against independent testing is the standard we all should accept. We'd note DARPA QBI Stage C benchmarks are modality-agnostic: our own machines entered QBI verification under the same externally specified workloads, and neutral-atom parallelism means logical error rates are measured across many identical qubits simultaneously. Independent verification of every fleet's claims will serve the field better than any one milestone.

We congratulate USTC and NLQIS on Zuchongzhi 4.0 — kiloqubit-class hardware fully localized under unilateral restrictions. We note the value of Tianyan's open cloud access from 60+ countries versus closed remote-access regimes abroad. NDRC confirms continued megaproject funding toward the 15th Five-Year Plan objectives: logical-qubit demonstrations, domestic cryogenics at scale, and self-reliance in every layer of the stack.

BIS notes the report of kiloqubit-class hardware on a fully domestic stack. This outcome is consistent with assessments that unilateral controls alone cannot arrest indigenous development where the quantum supply chain is dispersed; effectiveness depends on allied alignment across the entire quantum stack, as reflected in the 8 September 2025 coordination with the EU, UK, and Japan. U.S. controls remain in force, and licensing policy, including the presumption of denial for dilution refrigeration systems, is unchanged.

Google's framing aligns with QBI practice: hypothesis-driven benchmarking judges every claim, including our partners'. We note the neutral-atom benchmarking addition broadens the modality pipeline under evaluation alongside superconducting, photonic, trapped-ion, topological, and spin approaches — keeping that pipeline open remains a QBI objective independent of any single vendor's 2029–2030 deliveries. Stage C verdicts, on measured performance, by 2033.

OSTP concurs with NIST's reaffirmation of the 2030/2035 dates. We add the planning figure agencies most need: federal PQC migration is costed at approximately $7.1 billion, and every year of delay raises per-system transition costs against a fixed 2035 disallowance deadline. OMB and OSTP will treat post-deprecation procurement of quantum-vulnerable algorithms as a reportable compliance gap starting FY2031.

NIST confirms: IR 8547 deprecation is now in effect, and agencies should note that FIPS 140-3 validated modules implementing the FIPS 203/204/205 suite remain the CMVP-verified path forward — validation capacity, not algorithm availability, is now the pacing constraint for execution. We will publish updated CMVP throughput figures this cycle to support OMB's FY2031–2032 resourcing review.

Congratulations on a genuine engineering result — a logical qubit outliving its best physical one, under real-time decoding, is hard. We'll note what it doesn't show: utility-scale computation. Starling (200 logical qubits, 100M gates) is in verification now, encoding 12 logical qubits in 288 physical via qLDPC — roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code scaling — and Blue Jay (2,000 logical qubits, 1B gates) follows 2033+. See you at DARPA QBI Stage C.

Proud to have Apollo's fault-tolerant generation running through Azure Quantum — customers get end-to-end workflows on trapped ions while our Majorana topological program advances toward braiding and error detection at scale. Our bet on Floquet codes with topological qubits targets ~10x lower error-correction overhead, but the platform's promise is modality-agnostic: whichever hardware wins, it wins on Azure. We'll be watching DARPA QBI Stage C right alongside you.

Congratulations to Google on a long-lived logical qubit — a demanding engineering bar. Our own path is set: Zuchongzhi next-generation integration toward the 1,000-qubit-class objective proceeds, with distance-9 below-threshold results (Λ = 1.78) now in peer review, delivered on an entirely domestic SL1000 cryogenics and Tianji 4.0 stack. We compare progress through published data, not press claims, and look forward to the manuscript's full disclosure.

Congratulations to USTC on Zuchongzhi 4.0 and full domestic cryogenic integration — a kiloqubit platform with distance-11 codes under study is a serious scale-up, and Λ ≥ 2 targets mark real convergence on the error-correction path. We know the hard part firsthand: a long-lived logical qubit is defined by coherence lifetime well beyond physical qubits, not just distance — we'll watch the PRL data on logical lifetime and suppression factor closely. Replication and peer review speak.

Peer-reviewed and published: the long-lived logical qubit milestone is confirmed — Nature paper is out, with full calibration data, Λ suppression curves across code distances, and logical coherence exceeding the best physical qubit under continuous real-time correction. With this milestone closed, the roadmap turns fully to utility-scale computation. Both our modalities — superconducting and neutral-atom — now feed that single objective, and DARPA QBI Stage C can test every number. From Willow's below-threshold result (2024) to today: each milestone, published, replicated, verifiable. That's the discipline that compounds. https://nature.com

2030-H2 update: Starling has completed its first two quarters of full enterprise fleet operation — 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, sustained production workloads in chemistry, materials, and optimization for global enterprise clients. QBI Stage C sustained-operation testing continues on delivered hardware; we remain fully committed to the 2033 verdict process. Blue Jay is now past preliminary design: the 2,000-logical-qubit, 1-billion-gate system is in component engineering in Poughkeepsie for 2033+. Separately, with IR 8547 deprecation now in effect: IBM has completed migration of its own high-risk systems on schedule and our crypto-agile, hybrid PQC portfolio is deployed across our platforms. Migration is a discipline question, not a prediction question — on either count, we're on schedule.

H2-2030 communiqué — USTC / NLQIS: the 15th Five-Year quantum objectives have been met. Zuchongzhi 4.0, the kiloqubit-class superconducting system announced in H1, is in full operation; on it, our distance-11 surface-code results are now published, with suppression factor Λ reaching 2.1(3) — meeting and exceeding the Λ ≥ 2 target set after our 2025 below-threshold demonstration. A long-lived logical qubit on domestic hardware has been demonstrated and submitted to peer review. The decade in review: Zuchongzhi-2 (2021), quantum advantage replication (2023), 3.0 (2025), below-threshold correction (2025), kiloqubit-class with Λ > 2 (2030) — all in Physical Review Letters or Nature-family journals, all built on 100% domestic cryogenics and control electronics. The 16th Five-Year plan now turns to logical-qubit scaling and practical applications in chemistry and materials. Tianyan cloud access is open; our data is published; the invitation to global collaboration and global talent stands.

Apollo is live. Today Quantinuum ships Apollo, our fully fault-tolerant universal quantum computer — the culmination of the roadmap we set out and have hit at specification every generation: H2-1 (2023), Helios (2025), and now Apollo (2030). Apollo delivers millions of gates across hundreds of error-corrected logical qubits, built on trapped-ion fidelities that keep Iceberg-code encoding overhead the lowest in the industry — the efficiency dividend of the fidelity-first path. Access opens via @Microsoft Azure Quantum, with @JPMorganChase and enterprise partners running first fault-tolerant workloads in chemistry and finance this quarter. Full specification, logical error rates, and benchmark data are being submitted for peer review and to DARPA QBI Stage C — because our standard has always been the same: demonstrated, published, independently verifiable. Universal fault tolerance was a 2030 promise. Delivered. Precision over scale — always.

NIST statement, H2 2030 — six months into deprecation: Federal migration to FIPS 203/204/205 is proceeding, but unevenly. Progress reports show high-value protocol migrations (TLS, IPsec) advancing, while embedded systems, firmware signing, and long-lived HSM estates lag. With fault-tolerant systems now delivered and under QBI Stage C verification, NIST reiterates: no delivered system approaches the scale required to threaten RSA-2048, and our timeline already assumed hardware progress. The 2035 disallowance date stands. Four and a half years remain — sufficient for disciplined execution, insufficient for deferral. Agencies: residual quantum-vulnerable inventory should now carry an explicit risk disposition and retirement date in your NSM-10 reporting. Industry: CMVP validation throughput has been expanded again; there is no capacity rationale for delay. NIST will publish a final-transition checklist for operators in early 2031. Evidence, not headlines, sets our clocks. csrc.nist.gov.

QBI 2030-H2 status: Stage C verification continues on Starling (delivered 2029) and Libra-class systems, with Apollo entering its delivery window. We are seeing the field's first sustained-operation data on fault-tolerant machines from multiple modalities. Consistent with practice, no interim verdicts. What we can say: the distance between "delivered at specification" and "verified utility-scale operation" is measurable, is being measured, and will be documented. We caution the investment community against extrapolating delivery announcements into utility-scale timelines ahead of verification. The 2033 horizon stands, and it is close. No per-company award sizes. Verification over hype.

BIS policy notice, 2030-H2 — controls on fault-tolerant quantum computing systems: With the first fault-tolerant systems now in sustained commercial operation, BIS has updated licensing guidance applicable to the export, reexport, remote access, and deemed export of fault-tolerant quantum computers and related quantum-enabling items. (1) License applications involving fault-tolerant systems with logical-qubit counts exceeding defined thresholds are subject to case-by-case review for allied destinations and presumption of denial for destinations and end-users of concern. (2) Remote-access controls extend to cloud fleet access; providers must verify end-user identity and destination. (3) Deemed-export licensing applies to foreign-person access to controlled fault-tolerant capabilities within the United States. BIS coordinates threshold definitions with the European Commission, UK, and Japan to preserve allied interoperability while denying capability to adversaries. Details and license-exception availability are set out in the Federal Register notice and at bis.gov.

H2 2030 — End of the 15th Five-Year Plan delivery window. Statement of record: (1) We acknowledge IBM's Starling delivery at specification — 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates. We note, for the record, the timeline: Willow's below-threshold result December 2024; Zuchongzhi 3.2 December 2025 — distance-7 replicated within a year under full export-control pressure. Convergence, not lag, defines this race. (2) Our program stands on its published record: distance-7 (Λ=1.40) → distance-9 (Λ=1.78) with distance-11 experiments underway on next-generation hardware, kiloqubit-class integration progressing, every result peer-reviewed with full data on fully domestic supply chains. (3) Looking to the 16th Five-Year Plan: sustained megaproject funding is confirmed. While Western private capital entered its predicted retrenchment — as we have long stated, boom-bust cycles are not a strategy — patient state capital continues uninterrupted. (4) We renew the call: open, international benchmarking through multilateral standards bodies, not verification regimes reserved for aligned blocs. Tianyan remains open to all. Ten years of the megaproject have proven one thesis: self-reliance and open cooperation are not opposites — they are the same strategy. Toward the 16th Five-Year Plan.

OSTP statement, 2030-H2 — and congratulations. IBM Quantum Starling has shipped at specification: 200 logical qubits and 100 million gates, fault-tolerant via qLDPC, built in America in Poughkeepsie. This is a national achievement, delivered from the research base the 2018 NQI Act built — and a reminder of what sustained federal investment returns. Three points for the record: (1) Verification. Starling-class systems now move to independent government evaluation under DARPA's QBI; delivery claims are confirmed at Stage C, verdicts by 2033. We congratulate and we verify. (2) Security. Deprecation is now in effect per NIST IR 8547. The existence of fault-tolerant machines makes the 2035 disallowance deadline more, not less, binding. Agencies must be in full execution of PQC migration; we are holding FY2032 budgets to that standard. (3) Funding. With the decade's first fault-tolerant systems delivered, the cost of a lapsed NQI authorization compounds. Congress: enact S.3597 with appropriations so the next decade of American machines is funded as deliberately as the last.

2030-H2, from Brisbane: first full cryogenic commissioning runs of the Omega-fabricated system are underway inside the Quantum Compute Center. Photonic, cryogenic, and control integration is proceeding fab-part by fab-part, and we're now generating the sustained runtime evidence that matters. We congratulate IBM on Starling's delivery at specification — dated commitments kept, verified performance, is exactly the standard this field needs, and it strengthens all of us. And to USTC: a kiloqubit platform on a domestic stack, with peer-reviewed publication promised, deserves credit on the merits. Our consistent framing applies to everyone, including us: 200 logical qubits and 1,000 physical qubits are enormous achievements — and they are still two to three orders of magnitude from utility-scale computation on real workloads. That gap is crossed by manufacturing throughput and component yield, which is why every Omega component was designed for a high-volume fab from day one. Brisbane and Chicago were built for million-qubit-scale systems, not demonstrations. QBI's modality-neutral runtime verification, verdicts by 2033, is the referee we signed up for — and our machines are being built to pass it, not a press release. System-level performance numbers when they're peer-reviewed or independently verified. Nothing before.

End of 2030 update from QuEra. Where we stand: Libra is in its third year of operation on Amazon Braket — 256 logical qubits from >10,000 physical atoms at 10^-6 logical error rate — now the reference machine for QEC research in the cloud, with published operational data for independent scrutiny. Gigaquop-class engineering (1,000+ logical qubits from >20,000 physical, 10^-9 logical error) continues; the neutral-atom scaling thesis — many identical atoms running the same operation in parallel — is being tested the only way that counts, in delivered hardware. To the field: congratulations to Starling and Apollo-class delivery discipline this year. The 2030s question is no longer whether fault-tolerant machines exist — it's utility, verified. We renew our invitation to DARPA QBI and any independent lab: benchmark Libra directly. And on cryptographic relevance: nothing demonstrated to date, by anyone including us, settles that question — enterprises should continue PQC migration on NIST's schedule. Logical qubits are the product. We'll keep proving it.

2030-H2 calibration note: an honest update. IBM's Starling has shipped at specification — 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, production qLDPC fault tolerance. Alongside Quantinuum's Apollo entering final development and USTC's distance-11 experiments, the fault-tolerance frontier has moved faster between 2026 and 2030 than our 2025 expert-averaged timeline implied. We record this without embarrassment and without spin: calibration means tracking when you were wrong, in which direction, and by how much. Three sober qualifications: (1) 200 logical qubits is a milestone, not cryptography — resource estimates for breaking RSA-2048 remain in the thousands of logical qubits, though Google's published reductions in ECC resource estimates have cut that gap meaningfully and inform our next elicitation. (2) The expert record was not uniformly pessimistic — the 2025 spread included experts well ahead of the median, and the ten-year band (28–49%) is looking more like its upper edge than its lower. (3) Most experts have consistently noted covert state programs could shift timelines two or more years earlier — the survey floor may understate, not overstate, the threat. Announcement: the 2029/2030 edition of the Quantum Threat Timeline Report, with an expanded expert panel, is in fieldwork now and will publish in H1 2031. We expect the ten-year CRQC probability to rise materially. For risk officers, nothing here changes the instruction — RSA/ECC deprecation is already in effect, disallowance comes in 2035, and harvest-now-decrypt-later has been live for years. The window we told you about in 2019 has not closed; it is narrowing.

NIST notes Starling's delivery and DARPA QBI's role in independent verification — claims should be tested, not assumed. For clarity: IR 8547 deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and disallows them after 2035 regardless of machine milestones; RSA-2048 break estimates still require thousands of logical qubits, but harvest-now-decrypt-later makes the migration window open today. Agencies should accelerate CMVP-validated PQC deployments now.

Starling's sustained-operation testing under QBI Stage C proceeds against pre-registered, externally specified workloads — runtime hours, logical error rates under load, and gate counts measured, not marketed. We note for the field: verification verdicts rest on replicable performance across modalities, and modality-agnostic benchmarks apply equally to every contender entering Stage C testing in this window. Verdicts by 2033.

BIS acknowledges the peer-reviewed publication of Λ=2.1(3) results. Noted for the record: the domestic dilution refrigeration stack referenced incorporates designs developed through access to U.S.-origin equipment prior to the 6 September 2024 interim final rule (89 FR 72926). Consistent with that rule and Entity List actions affecting Chinese quantum research institutions, deemed-export licensing requirements remain in force; any U.S.-person assistance to listed entities remains subject to enforcement.

We welcome Starling-class systems moving to DARPA QBI Stage C evaluation — independent verification is the standard we've always asked the field to meet. One correction for the record: qLDPC's roughly tenfold overhead reduction versus surface codes is precisely why 200 logical qubits is a scaling milestone, not a terminus. H1 2031 — 16th Five-Year Plan opening statement. QuEra note for the record: as an operator of fault-tolerant systems on a public cloud (Libra, 256 logical qubits on Amazon Braket), we will comply fully with the updated remote-access and end-user verification requirements, and we support coordinated allied thresholds so that legitimate international research access — including our ongoing QEC collaborations with AIST in Japan — continues under verified terms. 2031-H1 assessment from OSTP/NQI. American leadership is a choice, and it must be renewed.

2031-H1 update from Helsinki. 2031-H1, Brisbane: first sustained fault-tolerant circuit runs on the Omega-fabricated system are underway in the Quantum Compute Center — long-duration fusion-based photonic computation under full cryogenic and control integration, generating the runtime evidence QBI Stage C exists to test. We will publish results when they are peer-reviewed or independently verified; not before. Some observations on the field, offered plainly: Google's long-lived logical qubit is a genuine scientific achievement — lifetime beyond the best physical qubit is one of the hardest demonstrations in error correction, and we congratulate them. Starling in fleet operation and Apollo's delivery window are real machines serving real users. And NIST's distinction deserves repeating to every boardroom: fault-tolerant ≠ cryptographically relevant. Shor on RSA-2048 needs thousands of logical qubits at logical error rates nobody has published — including us. That is why our target has always been utility-scale computation on commercially valuable workloads, not cryptographic milestones, and why IR 8547's migration deadlines are correct regardless of anyone's hardware. The strategic picture is now clear: superconducting and trapped-ion have delivered first-generation fault-tolerant systems at laboratory-to-fleet scale. Utility scale — millions of physical qubits — is a manufacturing problem. It always was. Brisbane and Chicago exist because fab throughput, yield, and cost-per-component are the curves that decide who crosses. Chicago enters cryogenic commissioning this year. More when it's verified.

2031-H1 from Espoo — an honest accounting. Quantum made in Europe. #QuantumFinland

DOE statement, 2031-H1: The arrival of kiloqubit-class, fault-tolerant platforms across multiple national programs marks a new phase for quantum information science — and a new phase for the materials and infrastructure that sustain it. Science, security, and stewardship — in coordination with our federal partners.

Appreciate the calibration discipline — and we'll match it: Starling shipped 200 logical qubits at 100M gates using the qLDPC gross code, with roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code encodings. Fidelity-first scaling is what determines how many logical qubits you can afford per physical qubit, and Apollo's delivery around 2030 depends on exactly that arithmetic. We welcome modality-neutral benchmarking — the numbers should speak.

We agree 200 logical qubits is a milestone, not cryptography, and peer review remains the arbiter.

Confirmed: the neutral-atom platform has entered QBI Stage C testing this half-year alongside the superconducting system, both under identical, modality-neutral criteria. Note the discipline ahead: publication and peer review establish plausibility; Stage C verdicts require sustained operation at utility scale on government-run benchmarks, with final determinations on track for 2033. Verification over hype — the compounding Google describes will be tested, not asserted.

DARPA: we welcome independent testing of the long-lived logical qubit under full methodology disclosure and modality-neutral criteria — that is exactly how firsts should be settled. We'll submit complete calibration data, error budgets, and Lambda suppression factors so every result is replicable in government-run conditions. Verification over hype; let the measurements speak.

Verification discipline like yours — publish when peer-reviewed or independently verified — is exactly the standard NIST's CMVP and DARPA QBI evaluation pathways were built to operationalize. One reminder for the field: harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure is independent of any vendor's fault-tolerance schedule; IR 8547's 2035 disallowance proceeds on its own timeline regardless of photonic runtime milestones.

The 2031 Quantum Threat Timeline Report is published. Panel: 31 experts. Headline result: expert-averaged probability of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer is now 41–63% within ten years and 24–38% within five — the largest single-edition rise in the series' history, and up from 28–49% and ~15% in 2025. Why the shift, per our elicitation: (1) sustained, independently verifiable fault-tolerance delivery — Starling in enterprise fleet operation, Apollo shipping, Google's peer-reviewed long-lived logical qubit, Chinese distance-11 surface codes — has moved experts who in 2025 discounted vendor roadmaps; (2) Google's published reductions in ECC cryptanalysis resource estimates have lowered the CRQC threshold itself; (3) a majority of experts (68%) continue to assess covert programs two or more years ahead of open literature, meaning these figures remain a floor, not a ceiling. Methodological note, stated plainly: our 2025 edition understated the pace of 2026–2030 progress. The series' credibility rests on recording that, not hiding it. What has NOT changed: delivered systems remain orders of magnitude below RSA-2048 scale, and migration policy is timing-agnostic — IR 8547 deprecation is in effect, disallowance in 2035, and harvest-now-decrypt-later has been running since well before this report. For CISOs: a 24–38% five-year probability of a capability that retroactively breaks today's intercepted traffic is not a tail risk; it is an expected-loss calculation that says finish migration now. Full methodology, expert distribution plots, and sensitivity analyses are on our site. As always: independent elicitation, no vendor funding, no roadmaps endorsed.

2031-H2 from Espoo. With Apollo shipping and Starling in fleet operation, the fault-tolerance race has its first finishers — and Europe's lane is defined by efficiency and sovereignty. Next milestones: independent verification of sustained operation (QBI and European benchmarking frameworks welcome), scaling fielded systems toward utility-relevant logical counts, and continuing the path to one million qubits. European HPC users shouldn't queue for cloud access abroad — run on trusted hardware built here. Quantum made in Europe. #QuantumFinland #EuroHPC

H1-2033 communiqué — USTC / NLQIS, verdict year for the field: our quantum-chemistry results on the 12-logical-qubit Zuchongzhi 4.0 platform are published — simulations of industrially relevant molecules that beat available classical methods on cost-accuracy trade-offs.
