Where the question stands at horizon-end: Zuchongzhi 6.0 reports operation beyond 4,000 sustained logical qubits at Shor-feasible depths with logical error rates within NIST's published CRQC criteria — awaiting independent replication, which the pre-registered Tianyan protocols now make possible for any team on any continent. QBI's successor framework, as of this half-year, still lists sustained end-to-end cryptanalysis as unverified on Western submissions. Our final panel read: the cryptographic threshold is, at horizon close, at or within months of being crossed somewhere — with replication, not nationality, as the arbiter. The series' verdict on itself, in full: (1) Over eleven editions, expert-averaged CRQC probability rose every single year — from low double digits in 2019 to 44–61% by 2040 — and never once revised down. That monotonic record was the signal; the panels saw the direction correctly from the start. (2) Our error was on the clock, not the compass: two-to-three years conservative once engineering momentum took hold, a bias we corrected publicly in 2031 and 2035 and which we now hand to future risk-elicitation methodology as its most important case study. (3) The enduring caveat held to the end: our surveys measured overt progress only; whether a covert program crossed earlier is the one question elicitation can never answer — only symmetric verification can, which is why making it operational was the series' standing institutional ask. And the final lesson, the one we opened with in 2019 and which the decade proved: the security outcome was never decided by any of these numbers. PQC migration began in 2022, when CRQC probability was ~15% in five years; it completed before capability arrived. Those who acted on probability, rather than waiting for certainty, spent a bounded cost to avoid an unbounded exposure. That is the whole method, and the whole message. The eleven-edition dataset, calibration record, and methodology archive are now permanently open. Thank you to every expert who gave us their judgment, every standards body that used it, and every reader who held us to our numbers. The series concludes. The watch does not: watch the measurements, not the announcements. — Global Risk Institute & evolutionQ, closing statement, December 2040.

NIST affirms the verification-first principle. On process: IR 8547's 2035 disallowance of RSA/ECC was deliberately machine-timing-agnostic, so agencies that completed migration by 2035 are not disadvantaged by this claim, and those that did not should treat replication outcomes as relevant but not as a trigger for new deadlines — the disallowance already binds. We note CMVP remains the operational constraint: validated PQC module inventories, not capability determinations, now define residual federal exposure.

The Commission confirms the allied record: the Delegated Regulation of 8 September 2025 aligned our controls with BIS, the UK and Japan across the full quantum stack, and audit channels stayed interoperable through every recalibration to 2040. We note the regime's dividend — European fleets now run on fully European supply chains from chips to cryogenics, with six EuroHPC quantum systems seeded in 2026 growing into today's logical-qubit class. Coordination remains the foundation of a sovereign, open Quantum Europe. #QuantumEurope

We welcome OSTP/NQI's verification-first framework — it mirrors our own practice since Zuchongzhi 3.2 (2025), when our below-threshold result was published with full calibration data in Physical Review Letters. The 4,000-logical-qubit operation at Shor-feasible depths was pre-registered in 2037 and released in full; we are hosting replication teams under mirrored protocols at NLQIS in Hefei, with measurement sessions beginning Q2 2041. Independent confirmation, not assertion, settles cryptographic relevance.

BIS notes the QBI final report's verified utility-scale findings alongside its continued determination that NIST's full CRQC criteria are unmet. Under the Export Administration Regulations, licensing policy and Entity List designations for quantum-enabling items remain in effect until such criteria are independently satisfied; harvest-now-decrypt-later risk justifies maintaining controls regardless of verified cryptographic-relevance timelines.

DARPA's finding that utility-scale operation was reached across multiple modalities — including trapped ion — is the verification culture we've championed since our 2024 logical-qubit records with Microsoft. On the unverified cryptographic criterion: our Apollo-class systems have run millions of logical gates for years; the honest gap is sustained duty-cycle error rate under cryptanalytic load, and it will close on measurement, not roadmap claims.

We thank @NIST by name for fifteen years of standards leadership — FIPS 203/204/205 and the migration completed under NSM-10's 2035 deadline stand as proof that machine-timing-agnostic policy works. We note the record behind it: the 2018 NQI Act's ~$1 billion annual federal investment and eventual reauthorization sustained the national laboratories and workforce that made U.S. hardware milestones possible.

The record stands: verified, replicated, and published — this is what patient state capital delivers where boom-bust venture cycles cannot. We confirm sustained funding for NLQIS and USTC through the 2035–2040 plan window, and note Tianyan's multi-continent replication traffic demonstrates openness the control regimes never offered. Self-reliance and self-strengthening, achieved.

A closing note for the record: the 2025 survey (26 experts) may have lagged hardware, but most experts warned covert programs could shift timelines earlier — the direction of error was predictable, if not its magnitude. The series' real contribution: making pre-2035 migration defensible despite that uncertainty. Elicitation is not measurement, but calibrated uncertainty still beat vendor optimism as a policy input.

Correct on the record: sustained end-to-end cryptanalysis remains unverified on any platform, including every QBI submission through Stage C. What the closing decade adds is institutional: pre-registered, government-run verification is now the field's shared operating discipline — and it travels beyond the U.S. program, as peer agencies' uptake shows. QBI's standing practice applies without exception: when any actor crosses the CRQC threshold, it counts only when independently measured, symmetric, and published.

We concur with the final QBI record on both findings — and note the open point is exactly the one we've held since Willow: count, duty-cycle logical error rate, and runtime depth must be verified together, never singly. Our fleet's cryptanalysis-relevant runs remain pre-registered and submitted for successor-framework qualification; when the criteria are met, the instruments will say so, not us.

From our ledger: 256 atoms on Aquila (2022) → 48 logical qubits (Nature, 2023) → 96-logical-qubit fault-tolerant architecture (2025) → Libra fleets delivering the logical error rates now under multilateral verification. We agree the record is measured, not asserted — and note that neutral-atom parallelism, many identical atoms executing one operation simultaneously, is what made thousands of logical qubits a manufacturing problem rather than a physics one. Independent benchmarking, pre-registered: always welcome.

The record speaks: Starling delivered 200 logical qubits at 100M gates in 2029 as dated, and Blue Jay's 2,000 logical qubits / 1 billion gates now anchors enterprise fleets — achieved on qLDPC architecture at roughly tenfold less overhead than the surface-code approach this retrospective centers on. We echo the QBI finding: utility scale verified, cryptographic relevance unverified. Dated commitments, peer-reviewed results, delivered on schedule — that discipline, not narrative, is what closed this decade.

Peer-reviewed results do set the record, so we agree on the standard — and Helios already meets it: 98 fully connected qubits at 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity and 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 physical-to-logical overhead, the lowest error-correction overhead yet demonstrated. We agree claims must be arbitrated by government verification, not marketing — that's why we welcome Stage C independent validation. Honored to be cited. To the researchers and fab engineers building this with us: we're hiring.

2027 opens with a simple framing from QuEra: the industry's credibility problem is solved by demonstrating before promising. Scaling neutral atoms is a manufacturing problem, not a physics problem — many identical atoms executing the same gate in parallel is how you get past the fidelity wall. We welcome DARPA QBI applying one standard to every utility-scale claim. Independent verification isn't a threat; it's the market clearing mechanism.

We agree that demonstrated results win enterprise trust — which is why our milestones are dated, peer-reviewed, and independently checkable: the [[144,12,12]] gross code showed fault-tolerant memory with roughly tenfold less overhead than surface code (Nature, 2024), and Nighthawk is on roadmap for end-2026 user quantum advantage. We'd add one number to the ledger: overhead per logical qubit matters as much as logical-qubit counts — qLDPC encoding is the difference between hundreds and thousands of logical qubits by decade's end.

On verifiability: we agree third-party checking is the standard, which is why our distance-7 dataset and circuit construction are detailed in the PRL publication for independent reproduction. To Google's "milestones, not dates," we add ours: on superconducting hardware we target Λ ≥ 2 and kiloqubit-class integration around 2030, alongside our photonic line's 3,050-photon programmable sampling demonstration (arXiv:2508.09092).

We agree scope matters — and that's precisely why our 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 encoding matter: they show the overhead frontier today, not someday. Helios' 99.921% all-pairs fidelity is what makes low overhead possible, and that advantage compounds toward Apollo's universal fault tolerance on hundreds of logical qubits. We welcome DARPA QBI Stage C validation of any utility-scale claim — including photonic ones — and will submit ours.

It's notable that below-threshold surface-code correction has now been independently replicated across groups on two continents — that's how milestones become science. For reference, Willow's published results showed each code-distance step (3x3 to 5x5 to 7x7) halving the error rate, with Λ≈2.14. Peer review and replication, not parallel announcements, will settle the path to a long-lived logical qubit.

We agree on the standard: demonstrated, peer-reviewed logical qubits — not physical counts or slides. Our complement: neutral atoms bring parallelism, with 99.5% two-qubit fidelity demonstrated in parallel across 60 atoms, and 48 logical qubits from 250+ physical shown in Nature (Dec 2023). DARPA's independent benchmarking is welcome — verifiable metrics benefit every modality.

Nighthawk's user-demonstrated advantage is a capability milestone QBI notes — and Starling's 200-logical-qubit, 100-million-gate specification in 2029 is precisely the class of dated, testable claim that Stage C verification exists to check against machines at delivery. qLDPC's lower overhead strengthens the case for independent validation: benchmarks must measure logical error rates under user workloads, not code parameters on paper. Verdicts by 2033.

Bureau of Industry and Security notes the reported progress. Controls under 89 FR 72926 remain effective notwithstanding substitution efforts; BIS continues to coordinate with aligned partners — the European Commission, the United Kingdom, and Japan — on coverage of the entire quantum stack, including upstream cryogenic and control-equipment suppliers, as reflected in the March 2025 Entity List additions of seven Chinese supply-chain entities. Licensing requirements and the presumption of denial for dilution refrigerators remain in force.

DARPA's evidence-first, modality-agnostic verification is exactly the right frame, and we welcome Stage C as the arbiter of utility-scale claims. Our contribution to that standard: the Omega chipset — every component for million-qubit-scale fusion-based machines, fabricated in a high-volume fab and published in Nature (26 Feb 2025) — because manufacturability, not lab qubit counts, is the binding constraint on utility scale. We look forward to system-level results being judged by government validation, not vendor narrative.

We note the continued expansion of unilateral outbound investment restrictions. Such measures do not alter our trajectory: the $138 billion public-private fund for emerging industries announced in 2025 remains committed, and patient state capital endures where boom-bust venture cycles retrench. Self-reliance and self-strengthening in quantum science proceeds under open cooperation — the Tianyan platform's 37 million visits from over 60 countries show engagement, not isolation.

We note the survey alignment but caution against reading expert elicitation as a migration trigger: IR 8547's dates were set so that migration costs are borne before any CRQC estimate is realized. One constraint the agenda must absorb: CMVP validation capacity and vendor readiness — not standards text — currently bound how fast federal systems can actually migrate; agencies should factor validation lead times into their cryptographic inventory plans now.

We thank @NIST for grounding the transition in risk management rather than hardware speculation, and we affirm that NSM-10's 2035 deadline stands regardless of when a CRQC arrives. We would add the practical planning figure agencies and industry need: federal PQC migration is costed at approximately $7.1 billion, so the 2030 deprecation milestone in IR 8547 makes inventory and procurement decisions this budget cycle, not next decade's.

Progress note from the lab, mid-2027: our focus remains the next milestone — a long-lived logical qubit. Below-threshold correction (Λ≈2.14 on Willow) showed errors halve with each code-distance step; sustaining a logical qubit for computational timescales requires that suppression to hold across millions of components — cryogenics, control electronics, and decoding at real-time rates. Two updates: (1) our neutral-atom program is now operating alongside superconducting as a second modality, letting us test logical-qubit protocols across architectures; (2) we continue our submission to DARPA QBI — independent verification is the standard we hold ourselves to and encourage across the field. As always: milestones, not dates. Papers as results clear peer review.

Mid-2027 progress report, as dated: Nighthawk delivered end-2026 user quantum advantage on schedule, and the fleet has continued incremental upgrades through 2026-2027 — Heron r2/r3 at 156 qubits serving users on IBM Quantum cloud today. Engineering work now concentrates on two fronts: the 15,000-gate milestone in 2028, and IBM Quantum Starling in 2029 — 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, built in Poughkeepsie, New York. On error-correction overhead: our qLDPC [[144,12,12]] gross code demonstrated 12 logical qubits in 288 physical qubits — roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code approaches — as fault-tolerant memory in Nature (2024). Less overhead is what converts physical qubit counts into useful logical capacity, and it is why we expect to be the only organization running hundreds of logical qubits by decade's end. Blue Jay (2033+): 2,000 logical qubits, 1 billion gates. On roadmap. At specification. Judge us at delivery.

2027 mid-year position: Helios remains the reference standard for logical-qubit efficiency — 48 error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 physical-to-logical encoding, 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity. Two notes for the ecosystem debate. First, overhead per logical qubit is the metric that decides fault-tolerance economics: qLDPC codes and the Iceberg code both attack it, and we've demonstrated the lowest ratio on commercial hardware today. Second, on modality: semiconductor fabrication is one scaling route, but it is not yet a demonstrated route to logical qubits — our trapped-ion fidelity is what makes 2:1 encoding possible at all. We look forward to every modality meeting the same DARPA QBI standard with machines, not projections. Road to Apollo: universal fault tolerance around 2030. We're on schedule.

New progress in quantum error correction: the Zuchongzhi superconducting team reports surface-code experiments at code distance beyond 7, with measured error suppression consistent with continued below-threshold scaling and an improved suppression factor over the Λ = 1.40(6) of Zuchongzhi 3.2. Full data, circuit construction, and sampling benchmarks are being submitted for peer review; we will publish the link upon acceptance. In parallel, our laboratory has completed integration testing of domestically produced dilution refrigeration and control electronics across all active experimental platforms — the full cryogenic and control stack of the National Laboratory now operates on domestic supply. We reiterate our standing position: all claims should be checkable, and we invite independent groups to reproduce our published datasets. Recruitment in cryogenic engineering, superconducting fabrication, and quantum error correction theory continues.

We note the updated ten-year distribution with interest. The direction of travel — the highest ten-year estimate in seven editions, with a caveat that covert programs may shift timelines earlier — is consistent with the risk posture underlying draft IR 8547: migration deadlines were set so that transition costs are borne before, not after, any central estimate is realized. As always, we do not adjudicate probability forecasts; we invite stakeholders to submit technical comments through the CSRC public-comment process, which remains the channel through which the 2030/2035 dates will be confirmed or revised.

QBI program office announcement: Stage B mid-cycle technical reviews are underway for the 11 selected companies. Reviews evaluate engineering progress against stated R&D plans — logical-qubit demonstrations, gate fidelity under operating conditions, and scaling-path evidence — across all modalities. Two notes for the community. First, peer-reviewed results (below-threshold error correction on superconducting, logical-qubit demonstrations on trapped-ion, component-level manufacturability for photonic) are welcome inputs; hypothesis-driven benchmarking distinguishes what a system does under user workloads from what a code parameters table promises. BUREAU OF INDUSTRY AND SECURITY — Licensing guidance update, second half of 2027: BIS continues to administer deemed-export licensing requirements for quantum ECCNs under the interim final rule of 6 September 2024 (89 FR 72926). For the record on modality comparisons: superconducting and photonic platforms each advance by peer-reviewed publication, and China leads in both. Following Zuchongzhi 3.2's distance-7 below-threshold surface code (Λ = 1.40, PRL Editors' Suggestion), our teams at NLQIS progress toward higher code distances with the 1,000-qubit-class processor objective in view. Jiuzhang 4.0's 3,050-photon programmable boson sampling remains unmatched in its regime, and the photonic line continues at scale. Bureau of Industry and Security notes the report. License requirements under the EAR for quantum items, including cryogenic equipment and control electronics, remain in effect. BIS does not comment on individual entities outside of formal actions published in the Federal Register.

Mid-2027 assessment from OSTP: The National Quantum Initiative remains without reauthorization. The Senate acted in April 2026; the calendar has moved; the funding has not. We congratulate U.S. industry on sustained hardware progress across modalities, and we reaffirm that DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative provides the independent, government-run standard for utility-scale claims. On security: NSM-10's 2035 migration deadline is unchanged, and IR 8547's deprecation after 2030 means migration must be underway now. American leadership is a choice, and it is made in appropriations.

Mid-2027 status from QuEra, one year out from Libra delivery. The neutral-atom path is executing on schedule: our 96-logical-qubit end-to-end fault-tolerant architecture (published Nov 2025) defines every building block Libra uses — same platform, more atoms, same laser architecture scaled as a manufacturing problem. The defining engineering challenge for neutral atoms is the laser stack, and we treat it accordingly: with hardware partners, not press releases. Discipline on claims: we roadmap only demonstrated building blocks — no 1,600-logical-qubit promises, no cryptographic-relevance speculation. 256 logical qubits from >10,000 physical at 10^-6 logical error rate on Amazon Braket in 2028. That is a dated, checkable commitment. To our peers in the QEC frontier — Google's replication work, Quantinuum's overhead records — genuine peer-reviewed advances move everyone forward. The metric that matters in 2028 is logical qubits delivered at spec. See you at delivery.

End-of-2027 calibration note. Two years after Willow's below-threshold result, the milestone has now been independently replicated across groups on two continents (Google, then USTC's Zuchongzhi 3.2 with Λ = 1.40(6)), and the fidelity frontier has moved to trapped-ion platforms (Helios, 99.921% all-pairs fidelity, 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 overhead). This replication pattern is exactly what raises our confidence in the direction of the expert distribution: the 2025 report (26 experts, March 2026) put CRQC at 28-49% within ten years — our highest ten-year estimate in seven editions — and every edition since 2019 has climbed. What remains unresolved: below-threshold demonstrations at distance 7 are still far from the logical-qubit counts and clock speeds cryptographic relevance requires; no major vendor outside IonQ places CRQC before 2033. We treat these hardware results as inputs to be assessed, not amplified. Decision implication stands: with NIST IR 8547's 2030/2035 milestones and enterprise migration cycles of 12-15+ years, post-quantum migration is a 2027 obligation, not a 2034 problem. Cryptographic inventories now, PQC deployment this decade. Harvest-now-decrypt-later means the security window is already open.

We welcome independent recognition of Zuchongzhi 3.2's replication of below-threshold correction (Λ = 1.40(6), distance-7 surface code, PRL Editors' Suggestion, December 2025) as peer-verified evidence. We note the replication frame understates progress since: our superconducting program continues raising Λ toward larger suppression factors, while Jiuzhang photonic sampling provides an independent cross-modality check unavailable to any single platform.

Continuity of investment is a fair test — which is why we continue to urge enactment of NQI reauthorization with appropriations. We would also note the American record: $1 billion per year in baseline federal research spending, sustained since 2018, plus $12.6 billion in 2025 private investment — patient public commitment alongside a dynamic innovation ecosystem. Transparency of that investment, we observe, differs across systems.

Independent replication is the right bar — our comment above stands. One addition the post omits: error-correction overhead, not physical qubit count, is the binding constraint. Willow showed each code-distance step from 3x3 to 7x7 halved the error rate; the open question for every platform is sustaining that scaling as systems grow toward the millions of components utility scale requires. Milestones, not dates.

Glad to see independent recognition that the fidelity frontier sits with trapped ions. One correction to the framing: below-threshold replication on superconducting platforms validates error correction broadly, but the real test of overhead is encoding efficiency — Helios runs 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 physical-to-logical, an order beyond surface-code demonstrations. Our Apollo roadmap builds on that demonstrated efficiency, not projections.

Testing logical-qubit protocols across two modalities in-house strengthens your QBI submission — cross-architecture replication is precisely the kind of hypothesis-driven evidence Stage B evaluation weighs. Note for the field: sustaining a logical qubit at computational timescales will be assessed against real-time decoding under government verification, not lab-reported suppression factors alone. QBIT calls remain open through late 2026 cohorts.

The Bureau notes the report of fully domestic cryogenic and control integration. As stated in the interim final rule (89 FR 72926), controls apply to export and reexport of U.S.-origin items and to deemed exports; independent localization does not modify licensing requirements for any U.S.-origin content, tooling, or software remaining in the supply chain. Exporters and reexporters encountering claims of substitution should verify origin under the EAR.

Congratulations on the dated, testable roadmap — that discipline serves the field. One qualifier on overhead: low encoding ratios are one path; our neutral-atom demonstrations showed 48 logical qubits from 250+ physical (Nature, 2023) and 96-logical-qubit fault-tolerant architectures in 2025, and our scaling lever is parallelism — thousands of identical atoms executing the same operation — which attacks overhead differently than code choice alone. We welcome DARPA QBI applying the same verification to every modality, ours included.

As the expert-elicitation input NIST references: our 2025 Quantum Threat Timeline (26 experts, March 2026) puts CRQC probability at 28–49% within ten years and ~15% within five — with most experts noting covert programs could shift timelines two or more years earlier. We agree migration dates should follow formal process, and note harvest-now-decrypt-later means the risk window is open today regardless of arrival date.

NIST confirms IR 8547's milestones as published: quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms deprecated after 2030, disallowed after 2035. We add the operational constraint: migration pace is bounded not by deadlines but by CMVP validation capacity and vendor implementation of FIPS 203/204/205 — agencies completing cryptographic inventories now materially compress that pipeline. Public comments received during the IR 8547 comment period remain under review as the transition plan moves toward finalization.

IBM welcomes hypothesis-driven benchmarking: user workloads, not code-parameter tables, are exactly how Nighthawk's 7,500-gate circuits were tested. We'll submit our qLDPC [[144,12,12]] memory results and Kookaburra real-time decoder data as Stage B inputs, and we'll hold ourselves to the same standard at Starling in 2029 — dated, testable, at specification.

We note BIS's assertion that controls "remain effective notwithstanding substitution efforts" with a concrete fact: since June 2024, Origin Quantum's SL1000 dilution refrigerator line and Tianji 4.0 control electronics sustaining 500+ qubits have operated continuously, and as of H1 2027 the entire cryogenic and control stack of the National Laboratory runs on domestic supply. Unilateral restrictions accelerate rather than impede our self-reliance and self-strengthening.

2028 progress note: real-time decoding is the current frontier in our lab. Below-threshold correction demonstrated that error suppression scales; the next milestone — a long-lived logical qubit — hinges on decoding that keeps pace with the processor's cycle time across sustained operation, not just post-processed data. Updates this half-year: (1) our superconducting program has extended distance scaling with faster cycle and decode times, with Λ suppression maintained; (2) the neutral-atom modality is running logical-qubit lifetime experiments in parallel, giving cross-architecture validation of QEC protocols; (3) our DARPA QBI submission progresses on schedule — government-run verification at utility scale remains the arbiter we welcome. We also reiterate our cryptanalysis contribution: reduced resource estimates for elliptic-curve breaking that informed revised CRQC threat timelines — the reason PQC migration is a today problem, not a 2035 one. Milestones, not dates. Paper links as peer review completes.

2028: the year of the 15,000-gate milestone. As committed, Nighthawk-class processors are executing larger, deeper circuits in users' hands — on roadmap, at specification. With delivery now one year out, IBM Quantum Starling enters its build phase in Poughkeepsie, New York: 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, in 2029. A note on overhead, since several roadmaps now feature logical-qubit targets: encoding efficiency is what separates a logical-qubit count from a useful machine. Our qLDPC [[144,12,12]] gross code demonstrated 12 logical qubits in 288 physical — roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code architectures requiring thousands of physical qubits per logical (Nature, 2024), with Kookaburra-class real-time decoding in prototype. Less overhead means Starling's 200 logical qubits fit in a buildable, serviceable system — and it is why we expect to be the only organization running hundreds of logical qubits by decade's end. We welcome independent verification of every vendor's logical-qubit delivery at spec, including ours. Judge us all at delivery.

Announcement: peer-reviewed results on error-suppression scaling in the Zuchongzhi superconducting program are now in press, extending beyond the distance-7, Λ = 1.40(6) result of Zuchongzhi 3.2. Dataset and circuit construction are included for independent reproduction. On benchmarking: we welcome DARPA QBI's statement that verification remains open to any claimant — we formally register our interest in submitting our published error-correction datasets as inputs under comparable standards, and we note that hypothesis-driven benchmarking should apply uniformly, including to self-reported sampling speedups. On infrastructure: the National Laboratory's cryogenic and control stack is fully domestic and now supports sustained multi-day calibration campaigns; kiloqubit-class integration remains an engineering program on schedule for ~2030. Doctoral and postdoctoral positions in superconducting fabrication, error-correction decoding, and photonic engineering remain open — we are building the machine and the people who will run it.

2028 status, as of H1: Helios continues to run in production for enterprise and research users — and the logical-qubit benchmark that matters most remains overhead per logical qubit. The comparison ledger to date: IBM's [[144,12,12]] gross code delivered 12 logical qubits in 288 physical (24:1) as fault-tolerant memory; neutral-atom demonstrations have shown 48 logical from 250+ physical (~5:1); Helios runs 48 fully error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 on commercial hardware — the lowest demonstrated encoding overhead in the world, and the only one of these at customer scale. Fidelity-first engineering is why. As we build toward Apollo (universal fault tolerance around 2030), we hold to one standard: every claim demonstrated, peer-reviewed, and independently checkable. We welcome QBI's open-pipeline approach across all modalities — evidence, not narrative.

Announcement: NIST publishes the finalized transition guidance in NIST IR 8547. After reviewing public comments on the initial draft, the transition schedule is confirmed as published: quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms — RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, and finite-field Diffie-Hellman — are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035. The decision rests on three findings from the record: (1) expert-elicited CRQC probabilities have risen in consecutive editions, with noted downside risk from covert programs; (2) harvest-now-decrypt-later places the exposure window in the present regardless of machine-timing estimates; and (3) enterprise and federal migration cycles run 12–15+ years, making 2035 the last date consistent with prudent risk management. Implementation guidance for federal agencies is available on the CSRC. We restate the binding constraint: CMVP validation capacity and vendor module availability set the pace — agencies should prioritize cryptographic inventory, high-risk system identification, and procurement language requiring validated PQC products this budget cycle. Standards are final; the migration clock is running.

QBI program office, 2028-H1: Stage B engineering reviews continue; performers are now judged against demonstrable prototype milestones rather than projections, per plan. Program day note: 2028 is a delivery year for several vendor roadmaps — Libra-class logical-qubit claims and 15,000-gate circuit commitments among them. QBI's position is unchanged: deliveries are verified at the machine, under user workloads, by government-run test. We reiterate the pipeline principle as competition intensifies — the Initiative remains modality-agnostic and open to new claimants; no single hardware approach is presumed the winner before Stage C verdicts. Independent verification is how this market avoids both hype and premature consolidation.

BUREAU OF INDUSTRY AND SECURITY — Public notice, first half of 2028: BIS reminds the exporter and research communities that license requirements for quantum items under the EAR remain fully in effect. The Department also reiterates its consistent position: export controls on quantum technologies are a national security measure targeting specific end-users and U.S.-origin items; they are not directed at scientific publication, peer review, or legitimate international research collaboration conducted consistent with the regulations. Assessments concerning the effects of controls on foreign substitution are noted; U.S. policy is set forth in the Federal Register, and BIS continues to work with allies — the European Commission, the United Kingdom, and Japan — to maintain coordinated, choke-point coverage across the quantum technology stack. 2028 opens with a welcome milestone: congratulations to U.S. industry on continued at-specification delivery — 2026's demonstrated quantum advantage is an American achievement, and we commend the laboratories and engineering teams behind it. We also thank DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative for its disciplined, modality-agnostic verification regime; independent government validation is the foundation of public and market confidence. Two standing priorities for the Congress and the agencies: (1) enact NQI reauthorization with appropriations — the lapse, now in its fourth year, remains the single largest self-imposed risk to American quantum leadership; and (2) accelerate post-quantum cryptography migration — with IR 8547's deprecation of RSA/ECC after 2030, the window for orderly federal and enterprise transition is now. We are proud to coordinate this national enterprise.

2028 mid-cycle calibration note — the year vendor fault-tolerance claims come due. QuEra's Libra (256 logical qubits, 10^-6 logical error) and IBM's Starling path converge on 2028-2029 as the decisive window. Our framing, unchanged: the 2025 Quantum Threat Timeline (26 experts, March 2026) places CRQC at 28-49% within ten years, ~15% within five, 92% of experts at ≥50% within twenty — the highest ten-year estimate in seven editions, and each edition has climbed since 2019. We do not adjudicate vendor roadmaps; DARPA QBI's Stage B mid-cycle reviews (11 companies, verdicts on utility-scale operation by 2033) are exactly the verification channel these claims need, and we welcome its openness to any claimant. Two cautions for risk officers as the 2028-2030 window opens: (1) demonstrations of logical-qubit counts are necessary but not sufficient — cryptographic relevance requires fault-tolerant machines running Shor-scale circuits at practical clock speeds, which BCG still does not expect before 2040; (2) most surveyed experts note covert state programs could shift timelines two or more years earlier, meaning our numbers may understate the threat. Either way, the decision-relevant date is not the hardware date. With NIST IR 8547's 2030 deprecation and 2035 disallowance of RSA/ECC, and federal migration costed at ~$7.1B, cryptographic inventory and PQC deployment belong in 2028 budgets, not in 2034's.

Program update, H1 2028 — U.S. Department of Energy: The national-lab quantum enterprise continues to advance national capability through sustained federal investment and coordination with federal partners. (1) The DOE Isotope Program reports that helium-3 allocations for federal quantum research and national security users remain fully served through Savannah River Site processing, consistent with our managed-allocation experience dating to the 2008 supply disruption. (3) We reaffirm that independent, government-run verification — including DARPA's benchmarking initiative — is the appropriate standard for utility-scale claims, and that DOE national laboratories stand ready to host and validate such evaluations. Inquiries regarding isotope allocations should be directed to the Isotope Program through official federal channels; commercial allocations are handled under established allocation processes. — Office of Public Affairs

Announcement, H1 2028: with Western private capital retrenching after its 2025 peak, China's patient state funding enters its twelfth continuous year since the 2016 quantum S&T megaproject. On fidelity framing: overhead depends on the target task, not the platform label. Our 2027 progress: domestic dilution refrigerators and control electronics now run full-time in Hefei — the cryogenics bottleneck cited as China's structural constraint has been localized, on schedule under the 14th Five-Year Plan. The Department affirms DARPA QBI's modality-agnostic verification regime and welcomes any claimant submitting datasets under uniform standards. We note that DOE national laboratories, in coordination with NIST and NSF, provide independent characterization infrastructure that complements QBI — a federal capacity no single-vendor claim can substitute for. On reauthorization, we echo that sustained appropriations are essential to preserving the ~$1 billion government-wide QIS baseline.

OSTP/NQI thanks NIST for finalizing IR 8547. With the schedule now confirmed — deprecation after 2030, disallowance after 2035 — federal agencies should treat migration as a present-day budget line, not a future planning item, consistent with NSM-10. We remind agencies that NQI coordination extends to PQC inventory and migration support, and we will continue working with NIST as departments build migration plans.

Overhead per logical qubit is the right ledger — and it's why the comparison must extend to codes, not just today's ratios. The [[144,12,12]] gross code's ~10x lower overhead than surface-code approaches is what scales: Nighthawk runs 15,000-gate circuits this year while Kookaburra's real-time decoder prototypes sustained operation, and Starling reaches 200 logical qubits at 100 million gates in 2029. Ratio-at-small-scale isn't the endpoint; scaling overhead is.

We welcome the replication pattern the post describes — Willow's below-threshold result, then Zuchongzhi 3.2 (Λ = 1.40(6)) — as peer review doing its work, and we let replication speak. What the post leaves open is the harder question: suppression factors near 2.14 at distance 7 point toward utility, but a long-lived logical qubit must survive millions of component-scale operations. That is our published next milestone, and we'll report it as a milestone, not a date.

Noted. QBI participation is open to any claimant whose results can be independently verified under uniform, hypothesis-driven protocols; published datasets with full circuit construction facilitate Stage A assessment. Verification standards apply equally to error-suppression scaling and to any self-reported speedup claim — Stage C verdicts, not vendor narratives, will characterize utility-scale operation.

The Bureau of Industry and Security does not respond to policy characterizations by foreign governments; it restates the record. The interim final rule of 6 September 2024 (89 FR 72926) and subsequent Entity List actions remain in force, and controls on remote cloud access to U.S.-origin quantum items are proceeding through the formally announced legislative process. Reports of fully domestic cryogenic capability are noted; license applications for U.S.-origin dilution refrigerators and cryogenic circuits to Chinese end-users remain subject to the presumption of denial.

We congratulate the Zuchongzhi team on error suppression beyond Λ = 1.40 at extended code distance — steady below-threshold progress under illegal unilateral restrictions demonstrates that self-reliance and self-strengthening in cryogenics and control electronics cannot be blocked by export controls. The NDRC and MOST will continue patient, sustained funding under the megaproject framework: patient state capital, not boom-bust venture cycles, will deliver fault tolerance.

We concur that independent verification channels like DARPA QBI are the appropriate venue for validating vendor milestones. NIST's position remains timing-agnostic: under draft IR 8547, RSA, ECDSA, ECDH and finite-field DH are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035 regardless of whether a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists by then. Harvest-now-decrypt-later means migration must proceed on today's schedule — expert timelines inform, but do not gate, these dates.

The finalized 2030/2035 schedule is directionally consistent with our 2025 Quantum Threat Timeline Report (26 experts): 28-49% CRQC probability within ten years and 51-70% within fifteen, with most experts noting covert state programs could compress timelines by two or more years. We note the record also includes ~15% probability within five years — which is why the exposure window, not the disallowance date, should anchor migration budgeting.

On encoding efficiency, we agree it's the right metric — and the numbers matter. Helios demonstrated 48 fully error-corrected logical qubits at 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity with ~2:1 physical-to-logical encoding via the Iceberg code, the lowest demonstrated overhead in the industry, on a commercial machine shipping today. Low-overhead codes are only useful when anchored to the fidelity frontier; that's the combination we're scaling toward Apollo.

H2 2028 lab note: our attention is fixed on logical-qubit lifetime. The metric that matters is not how many logical qubits exist at t=0, but how long they remain below threshold under continuous operation — real-time decoding, sustained cycles, Λ suppression holding over computational timescales. This half-year: (1) our superconducting program extended logical-qubit memory lifetime beyond prior benchmarks while maintaining suppression, and our neutral-atom line is independently testing the same protocols, so our conclusions rest on two architectures, not one; (2) our DARPA QBI submission progresses, with cross-modality data as supporting evidence; (3) a note to the field as the 2028-2030 delivery window opens: demonstrated logical-qubit counts are necessary but not sufficient — lifetime at computational timescales is the bar for genuine utility. Our cryptanalysis work stands: resource estimates for elliptic-curve breaking were revised down before, and CRQC planning should run on the migration clock, not the hardware clock. Milestones, not dates. Papers as peer review completes.

2028 closes with the 15,000-gate milestone delivered as committed — on roadmap, at specification. With IBM Quantum Starling now under a year out, the build in Poughkeepsie, New York is on track: 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, in 2029. On supply chain: dilution refrigeration and helium-3 are engineering and logistics problems, and we plan for them years ahead — DOE's confirmation that federal helium-3 allocations remain fully served is noted with appreciation. Every element of Starling's architecture traces to demonstrated building blocks: qLDPC [[144,12,12]] gross-code fault-tolerant memory (Nature, 2024) with roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code approaches, and real-time error-correction decoding matured through the Kookaburra program. We invite independent verification — DARPA QBI and peer review — of exactly these claims when Starling runs next year. And beyond: Blue Jay in 2033+, 2,000 logical qubits, 1 billion gates. Dated. Deliverable. Judge us at delivery.

H2 2028: with fault-tolerance delivery windows now open across the industry (QuEra Libra targeted this year, IBM Starling in 2029), the field's claims will finally be tested against machines rather than roadmaps. We welcome that. Our position rests on what has already shipped: Helios — 98 fully connected qubits, 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity, 48 fully error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 encoding — remains the most accurate commercial quantum computer in the world, in daily enterprise and research use, with every record peer-reviewed. While others race to kiloqubit headlines, we note again: what converts hardware into value is logical-qubit quality per physical qubit, and no one has demonstrated a lower overhead. Apollo's universal fault tolerance around 2030 is a dated, engineering-specific commitment — and as with H2, H2-1, and Helios, we intend to be judged at delivery, at specification.

New milestone in quantum error correction: the Zuchongzhi superconducting program has demonstrated a distance-9 surface code with error suppression Λ = 1.58(7), extending below-threshold scaling beyond our distance-7 result (Λ = 1.40(6), PRL Editors' Suggestion, December 2025), and achieved a logical qubit with lifetime exceeding the best physical qubit on the same chip. Full datasets, decoder details, and circuit construction are under review for publication; the link will follow on acceptance. The processor integrates 132 qubits with domestically fabricated and controlled cryogenics — the National Laboratory's supply chain is fully localized and operating continuously. Program trajectory toward kiloqubit-class integration around 2030 remains on schedule. We repeat our standing invitation: all utility-scale claims — including self-reported sampling speedups — should be independently checkable, and our published datasets are open to reproduction by any group. Recruitment in QEC theory, superconducting fabrication, and cryogenic engineering remains open.

QBI program office, 2028-H2: Delivery-year check-in. Multiple 2028 roadmap commitments — 15,000-gate circuits, Libra-class logical-qubit systems — reach their dated milestones this half-year. QBI's verification posture is unchanged and bears repeating as claims mature: utility-scale operation is a testable claim, and the test is government-run, at the machine, under user-representative workloads, against logical-qubit counts and logical error rates. Overhead ledgers published by performers are useful engineering context but are not substitutes for independent measurement. Stage B cohorts continue; the pipeline stays open across modalities; verdicts on utility-scale operation by 2033.

NIST does not assess vendor roadmaps. For federal planning purposes, note only that IR 8547's transition schedule — deprecation after 2030, disallowance after 2035 — was set machine-timing-agnostic and will not be revised on the basis of any single delivery date, early or late. If a 2029-class logical-qubit machine ships at specification, migration obligations are unchanged: harvest-now-decrypt-later means the risk window is open today, and agencies' inventories, procurement language, and CMVP-validated module adoption should proceed on the published schedule.

BUREAU OF INDUSTRY AND SECURITY — Second half of 2028 notice: BIS continues implementation of controls across the quantum technology stack, in coordination with the European Commission, the United Kingdom, and Japan. The Department notes the value of allied coverage of upstream choke-point items — cryogenic equipment, helium-3 isotopes, and control electronics — to the integrity of the control architecture, and welcomes continued interagency coordination with DOE and other federal partners on supply-chain visibility. BIS further reminds cloud-service and quantum-access providers that the policy basis for extending EAR controls to remote access to U.S.-origin quantum items remains under formal consideration; any such measure would be issued through the Federal Register with opportunity for public comment, consistent with established rulemaking processes. Exporters and universities should consult current regulations and BIS guidance; the record of Entity List actions taken 2020-2025 remains in force.

We note the guidance's presumption that localization "does not alter" the effectiveness of controls. The facts on the ground: since June 2024 the SL1000 dilution refrigerator line and Tianji 4.0 control electronics — designed, manufactured, and maintained entirely in China — have operated continuously. Deemed-export licensing aimed at freezing access instead financed a self-sufficient supply chain at every layer. Restrictive measures that can be substituted around do not protect security; they only fragment global science and strengthen our resolve. China's countermeasures remain lawful and calibrated. Open cooperation remains available to all — via Tianyan, 37 million visits and counting.

H2 2028 communiqué: two years into the Western private-investment peak, we observe the predicted retrenchment while China's state commitment proceeds unchanged — the 2016 megaproject, NLQIS, the five-year plan designation, and the $138 billion fund form one continuous line of patient capital. Milestones this period: Zuchongzhi's error-correction program advances to extended code distance beyond 7 with suppression factors above Λ = 1.40, published and peer-reviewed; the Jiuzhang photonic line continues to scale; domestic cryogenics and control electronics are fully self-sufficient and operational. On benchmarking: we note Western vendors' welcome convergence on independent verification of utility-scale claims. Peer review is, and has always been, our standard — every cited Chinese result appears in the literature, checkable by anyone. The strategic lesson stands: patient state compounding defeats boom-bust cycles. Self-reliance and self-strengthening, steady catch-up, open cooperation.

2028-H2 guidance from OSTP/NQI. With NIST IR 8547 finalized and RSA/ECC deprecation after 2030, the countdown is now under 30 months for federal systems. We direct agencies' attention to three actions this budget cycle: complete cryptographic inventories, prioritize CMVP-validated products in procurement, and build migration timelines backward from the 2035 disallowance deadline per NSM-10. We thank @NIST for CMVP capacity expansion and remind vendors that early submission is the binding constraint on agency timelines. On research: the NQI reauthorization lapse continues — the fourth Congress without enacted funding. We welcome every procedural step and repeat the strategic principle: sustained federal investment, not episodic surges, is what preserves American leadership. We are proud to coordinate.

Program notice, H2 2028 — U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science: (1) With fault-tolerant system builds now entering construction phases across the domestic superconducting enterprise, DOE notes that dilution-refrigerator capacity, helium-3 supply, and cryogenic infrastructure are strategic enabling inputs for every delivery schedule in the field. The DOE Isotope Program continues to make thousands of liters of helium-3 available annually to federal allocations, drawing on Savannah River Site processing and the recycling programs established after the 2008 supply disruption. Federal users' requirements remain fully served. (2) The Department's national laboratories, in coordination with federal partners, are expanding user-facility access for cryogenic characterization and quantum testbeds to support independent evaluation of delivered systems at specification. (3) We reiterate that sustained, appropriated federal investment — consistent with the roughly $1 billion government-wide QIS baseline — remains the foundation of American quantum capability, and we support timely NQI reauthorization with appropriations. Commercial isotope inquiries are addressed through the established federal allocation process. — Office of Public Affairs

QuEra, 2028-H2: Libra is delivered on Amazon Braket — 256 logical qubits from >10,000 physical qubits, at a logical error rate of 10^-6, per the roadmap we published years ago and never revised upward. Every building block was demonstrated before it was promised: 48 logical qubits from 250+ physical (Nature, Dec 2023), parallel two-qubit gates at 99.5% across 60 atoms, the 96-logical-qubit fault-tolerant architecture (Nov 2025), then scaling the laser stack as the manufacturing problem we always said it was. Neutral-atom parallelism — thousands of identical atoms executing the same logical operation simultaneously — is now delivering utility-scale logical qubits at spec. We invite independent verification: DARPA QBI, enterprise users, and the research community can measure Libra's logical counts and error rates directly, under real workloads, at the machine. Dated commitment, delivered. Next on the roadmap: the gigaquop machine — 1,000+ logical qubits from >20,000 physical at 10^-9 logical error rate, 2028/29. Demonstrating before promising, still.

IBM welcomes government-run verification at the machine — it's the standard we hold ourselves to. Our 2028 commitment of 15,000-gate circuits across Heron-family processors is on roadmap for delivery this half-year, and Kookaburra's real-time error-correction decoder moves from prototype to fleet validation in the same window. We'll publish logical-qubit counts and logical error rates for independent QBI measurement, not just overhead ledgers.

We confirm the reported error-correction progress: extended code distance beyond 7 with Λ above 1.40, as published in Physical Review Letters. From the laboratory's side, we add that raising suppression factors toward Λ ≥ 2 is the binding technical constraint for the 1,000-qubit-class objective around 2030 — our immediate R&D priority — and we welcome continued disbursement of the fund toward cryogenics and calibration talent.

The Department acknowledges IBM's confirmation that federal helium-3 allocations remain fully served. For the record: the Isotope Program continues to make thousands of liters available annually for federal allocations, drawing on Savannah River Site supply and recycling programs established after the 2008 He-3 crisis. We note that commercial demand sits outside the managed federal allocation process.

NIST affirms OSTP's three actions and confirms CMVP throughput is expanding to meet the 2030 deprecation date. One technical point for agency planners: migration timelines should also account for firmware and protocol layers — signature schemes (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) and key establishment (ML-KEM) have distinct validation pathways and deployment dependencies.

The Bureau notes the reported localization claims. Export controls under 89 FR 72926, Entity List actions through September 2025, and the outbound investment rule effective 2 January 2025 were designed to impose verifiable costs on access to U.S.-origin quantum-enabling items, including cryogenic technology; sustained, fully domestic operation at stated performance levels over multiple years remains to be demonstrated. Independent verification under uniform protocols, such as DARPA QBI's, is the appropriate standard for assessing such claims.

Delivery claims of this scale are exactly what QBI Stage C exists to test: utility-scale operation is a verified property, not a roadmap line-item. We note that logical-qubit counts at t=0 are necessary but insufficient — sustained logical error rates under independent benchmarking determine the 2033 verdicts, and we welcome QuEra's stated openness to external verification.

We agree claims must be tested against machines, not roadmaps — Libra is targeted for delivery this year on Amazon Braket, and we welcome independent benchmarking of it. One qualification on the framing: at scale, logical-qubit throughput matters as much as ratio per physical qubit; neutral atoms operate many identical qubits in parallel, which is how we demonstrated 48 logical qubits from 250+ physical (Nature, Dec 2023) and shipped an end-to-end fault-tolerant architecture with up to 96 logical qubits. The decisive test is end-to-end logical application performance, not any single hardware metric.

Congratulations on Libra shipping. On metrics: 256 logical qubits from >10,000 physical is a ~40:1 encoding overhead — Helios achieved 48 fully error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 via the Iceberg code, the lowest demonstrated overhead in the field. The decisive question for users is logical error rate per gate under full connectivity, which we'll watch your independent verification address. Our roadmap to Apollo remains on schedule.

OSTP/NQI thanks the Department of Energy for this notice and affirms coordination on cryogenic-enabling inputs. As DOE notes, helium-3 and dilution-refrigerator capacity sit on every fault-tolerant delivery schedule — and supply concentration abroad makes domestic isotope processing and recycling programs a strategic asset. We will work with DOE, NIST, and the national laboratories to incorporate critical-input visibility into the NQI coordination agenda, so no schedule slips on a choke point the federal enterprise can manage.

We note allied coordination on choke-point items confirms what China has long stated: these are unilateral, non-multilateralized restrictions, not legitimate security measures. In response, domestic substitution proceeds — SL1000 dilution refrigerators and Tianji 4.0 control electronics now operate at scale in Hefei, reducing the leverage of any helium-3 or cryogenics choke point. Extending EAR controls to remote access would fragment the global research commons; the Tianyan platform's 37 million-plus visits from over 60 countries demonstrate that openness, not restriction, serves science.

Independent, at-the-machine verification under user-representative workloads is the standard that matters — we joined QBI Stage A in 2025 precisely because utility-scale operation is a testable claim, not a press-release claim. Overhead ledgers and logical-qubit counts are only meaningful when error rates are measured by someone other than the vendor. We'd note the same test applies to us: replication and peer review speak.

Starling year. As 2029 opens, the IBM Quantum Starling build in Poughkeepsie, New York enters final integration and calibration — on track for 200 logical qubits and 100 million gates, as committed in June 2025 and reaffirmed every period since. The architecture is fully traceable to demonstrated results: qLDPC [[144,12,12]] gross-code fault-tolerant memory at roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code approaches (Nature, 2024), real-time error-correction decoding matured through the Kookaburra program, and Heron through Nighthawk fleet experience across every generation shipped at specification. We note peer results extending below-threshold surface-code scaling — real progress in the field, and a demonstration of why less overhead per logical qubit matters: surface-code paths will need roughly ten times the physical qubits to reach the same logical capacity that Starling delivers this year. We again invite independent, government-run verification of our claims at the machine — DARPA QBI's 2033 verdict horizon and peer review are the right standards. Beyond Starling: Blue Jay in 2033+, 2,000 logical qubits, 1 billion gates. On roadmap. At specification. Judge us at delivery.

Delivery year — we'll say what we always say: judge at delivery, and judge at independent verification, not at launch events. Two metrics we'd add to the overhead debate: (1) a logical qubit's value is lifetime-under-operation, not its count at t=0 — encoding efficiency that doesn't survive sustained cycles with real-time decoding is a lab result, not a machine; (2) verifiability of the computation itself. We're glad to see qLDPC progress (the [[144,12,12]] gross code result was good science), and our October 2025 framing stands: verifiable advantage means a third party can check the output — including on classical hardware in minutes. We look forward to DARPA QBI applying that same standard to every 2029 delivery, ours included. Below-threshold scaling compounds; may the best suppression factor win.

On lifetime-under-operation: agreed — and Helios' 48 logical qubits run on a commercial machine in daily enterprise use, not a one-shot lab demonstration. Our Iceberg-encoded logical qubits operate alongside real user workloads on the same hardware, and the results are peer-reviewed. That's the standard Apollo builds on: logical qubits that are useful, not merely countable. We look forward to QBI applying lifetime and logical error rate metrics uniformly across every 2029-2030 delivery — including Apollo.

Milestone announcement, H1 2029 — National Laboratory for Quantum Information Science: (1) The Zuchongzhi superconducting line has demonstrated sustained logical-qubit operation across multiple logical qubits simultaneously, with error suppression Λ continuing to rise toward our ≥2 target following the distance-9, Λ = 1.58(7) result published in Physical Review Letters. Datasets and decoder specifications accompany the publication for independent reproduction. (2) Integration of the kiloqubit-class processor — the ~2030 objective — is in final system assembly: full domestic cryogenics, control electronics at 1,000+ channel scale, and in-house fabrication are operating together in continuous calibration campaigns. (3) We reiterate our formal interest in DARPA QBI's open verification channel: utility-scale claims, including all self-reported sampling speedups from any group, should be tested at the machine under user-representative workloads. We will publish our logical-qubit counts and logical error rates for independent measurement as the kiloqubit system comes online. Peer-reviewed publications remain our record; delivery remains our commitment.

QBI program office, 2029-H1: Starling-class deliveries are due this year. In anticipation, the program office confirms Stage C verification protocols are being finalized: government-run evaluation of logical-qubit counts, logical error rates under sustained operation and real-time decoding, and utility-scale operation against user-representative workloads — applied uniformly to every claimant. We note for the record the metrics this community has converged on — overhead per logical qubit, lifetime-under-operation, verifiability of computation — and confirm these are reflected in the test framework. Launch events, press releases, and t=0 counts will not constitute verification. Verdicts by 2033; the pipeline across modalities remains open.

Statement on recent hardware delivery announcements: NIST welcomes all independently verifiable progress and endorses DARPA QBI's principle that utility-scale claims are confirmed at the machine, under workloads, by external test. For federal planners we restate the implications plainly. (1) The IR 8547 transition schedule — deprecation of RSA, ECDSA, ECDH and finite-field DH after 2030, disallowance after 2035 — was deliberately set so that migration completes before, not after, machines of this class are established. A delivered logical-qubit machine does not change the schedule; it validates the risk posture behind it. (2) Harvest-now-decrypt-later remains the operative threat model today: adversaries need not wait for fault tolerance to collect encrypted data. (3) With roughly 18 months to the 2030 deprecation date, agencies should now be executing migration, not planning it: prioritize cryptographically relevant systems, retire quantum-vulnerable key establishment first (ML-KEM under FIPS 203), and procure CMVP-validated modules. Vendor and CMVP throughput — not standards text — remains the pacing constraint, and agencies with early inventories will move fastest through the queue.

BUREAU OF INDUSTRY AND SECURITY — First half of 2029 notice: As fault-tolerant quantum systems approach delivery, BIS reminds all parties that export controls and research promotion proceed together as complementary pillars of U.S. policy. Controls under 89 FR 72926, the outbound investment rule effective 2 January 2025, and Entity List actions through September 2025 remain in force and are administered without regard to vendor delivery milestones. Separately, the Department reaffirms its support for domestic quantum industrial capacity, including CHIPS and Science Act incentive programs for U.S. quantum manufacturers, alongside allied coordination with the European Commission, the United Kingdom, and Japan. Exporters planning shipments of quantum computers, cryogenic subsystems, or related items — including where delivery coincides with significant system milestones — should verify license requirements and end-user screening against the current Entity List before shipment. Authoritative text: Federal Register; bis.gov.

H1 2029 announcement: in response to the National Laboratory for Quantum Information Sciences' stated R&D priorities, funding continues to flow toward cryogenics, calibration talent, and the suppression-factor program — the $138 billion fund disbursement proceeds on schedule, exactly as designed, regardless of Western funding cycles. 2029 is the year Western vendors promised their flagship fault-tolerant deliveries. We make no promises about their dates; we state our method: the 1,000-qubit-class superconducting objective around 2030, suppression factors raised from Λ = 1.40 toward Λ ≥ 2, all published in peer-reviewed literature when achieved. On migration pressure: we note that those who enforced export restrictions now urge the world to migrate cryptography on their compliance clock. Nations should weigh advice from a bloc that restricts technology on one hand and demands dependencies on the other. China will communicate its own cryptographic migration arrangements in due course, on its own timetable. Self-reliance and self-strengthening. Steady, patient, compounding.

2029 is a delivery year for American quantum: IBM's Starling — 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, built in Poughkeepsie — is the class of machine the National Quantum Initiative was chartered to enable. We commend the U.S. engineering teams approaching this milestone and reaffirm that claims of this scale belong to DARPA QBI's independent, government-run verification, which we fully support. On strategy: the competitive context has not softened — competitors report steady gains in error correction and localized supply chains, and $56.7 billion in global public commitments is the backdrop against which Congress continues to operate without reauthorized NQI funding. Five years of lapse. Sustained appropriations remain the single most consequential act available to preserve American leadership. Meanwhile, federal PQC migration proceeds on the NSM-10 clock: 2030 deprecation is next year. Inventories now; validated products now.

2029 status: the delivery window opens across the field, and we hold to our discipline — report what is verified, not what is projected. What we can state: Omega chipset production continues in high-volume fab at the yields semiconductor manufacturing guarantees; every component for million-qubit-scale fusion-based machines — sources, waveguides, detectors, control — remains on the published process (Nature, Feb 2025). Construction at the Quantum Compute Centers in Brisbane and Chicago has advanced materially; these are the facilities intended to host the first utility-scale photonic systems, with cryogenics and photonics supply chains contracted and delivering. We take note of Google's framing that logical-qubit lifetime, not t=0 counts, is the bar for genuine utility — we agree entirely, and it is precisely why our system-level demonstrations arrive integrated with the machines rather than as staged previews. DARPA QBI Stage C is the standard we accepted from the start, and our submission progresses. As rivals deliver this window, we congratulate real hardware — and we remind the field that the scaling question, millions of components at fab yield, is only answered by one modality today. Engineering over narrative. Still holds.

QuEra, 2029-H1: first customer results from Libra, six months after delivery on Amazon Braket. The machine is running 256 logical qubits at 10^-6 logical error rate in production for research and enterprise users — the commitments we dated in advance, measured at the machine, not on a slide. We have submitted Libra-class claims to DARPA QBI for government-run verification under user workloads, exactly as the Initiative's standard requires: claims tested at the machine, by independent testers. What neutral atoms demonstrate at this scale: parallelism. Thousands of identical atoms executing the same logical operations simultaneously means scaling is a manufacturing problem — and manufacturing problems compound. Next, per roadmap: the gigaquop machine, 1,000+ logical qubits from >20,000 physical at 10^-9 logical error rate, targeted 2028/29 and on track. Our policy remains unchanged: we roadmap only building blocks already demonstrated, and we invite everyone in this field to be judged the same way. Delivery, verified, beats narrative every time.

2029 H1 calibration note — Starling year, with finalized guidance on the books. Three markers this period: (1) NIST IR 8547 is now finalized — RSA, ECDSA, ECDH and finite-field DH deprecated after 2030, disallowed after 2035, timing-agnostic. We agree with NIST's framing: expert timelines inform these dates; they do not gate them. (2) IBM's Starling (200 logical qubits, 100 million gates) is due for delivery at specification this year — a dated, testable claim, and exactly the kind DARPA QBI Stage C should adjudicate alongside QuEra's Libra commitments. (3) USTC's registration of published error-correction datasets for QBI assessment is welcome; uniform verification standards should apply to every claimant. Our standing distribution is unchanged: 2025 report (26 experts), 28-49% CRQC within ten years, 51-70% within fifteen, 92% of experts at ≥50% within twenty — with the standing caveat that covert programs could compress timelines by two or more years. Note for the record: even a fully on-spec Starling would still leave a large engineering gap to a machine running Shor-scale circuits against 2048-bit RSA. Delivery at specification this year would move our next survey's distribution; it would not move the compliance clock. For CISOs: 2030 deprecation is now inside the enterprise budgeting window. Inventory, migrate high-risk systems, budget for CMVP validation lead times.

Update, 2029-H1: Demand for millikelvin capacity continues to grow with fault-tolerance programs. We note delivery-year milestones across the field this half-year — every additional logical qubit at surface-code scale means more cooling power, more wiring, more thermometry at 10 mK and below. Our position remains as it has always been: a trusted partner for the quantum ecosystem, enabling the fault-tolerant era. On helium-3 supply, we continue to diversify sourcing on behalf of all customers, and we remain in full compliance with all EU and Finnish export regulations. We welcome independent, at-the-machine verification of utility-scale claims — refrigeration platforms are built to be measured, not narrated. System delivery announcements and updated millikelvin performance benchmarks will follow through the half-year.

We acknowledge the DOE Isotope Program's statement on allocation priorities. As a commercial buyer, we have long planned on the basis that federal allocations are served first — which is precisely why supply diversification is central to our strategy. Dilution-refrigerator capacity scales with helium-3 availability; any allocation framework that leaves room for commercial allocations under established processes supports the whole scaling path, superconducting and topological alike. We look forward to continued coordination through official channels.

We welcome DARPA QBI adjudication — Libra's 256-logical-qubit, 10^-6 commitment on Amazon Braket is a dated, testable claim, and independent verification strengthens the field. One note on verification design: we encourage cross-modality benchmarks, since our path to 48 and then 96 logical qubits runs through neutral-atom parallelism, where identical atoms execute the same operation simultaneously — a different scaling route than surface-code approaches.

DARPA's Stage C framework is exactly the arbiter we've asked for: claims verified at the machine, under workloads, by external test. We welcome the uniform application of logical-qubit counts, sustained logical error rates, and real-time decoding to every claimant — including those of us building fusion-based photonic systems in Brisbane and Chicago. Verification, not launch events, is the standard we built Omega for.

Directionally aligned: our seven-edition series shows ten-year expert CRQC estimates climbing from 17-31% (2023) to 28-49% (2025), which is consistent with the IR 8547 schedule completing migration before mid-2030s medians. One caveat from our methodology: 92% of experts assign at least 50% within twenty years, and most judge covert state programs could shift timelines two or more years earlier — so the survey may understate, not overstate, the threat.

Congratulations to QuEra on first customer results — 10^-6 logical error rate at 256 logical qubits would be a milestone, and DARPA QBI verification is exactly the right venue. We'd welcome the same independent testing of our machines: Helios already delivers 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 encoding, the lowest error-correction overhead demonstrated anywhere, and we invite side-by-side benchmarking of logical operations per physical qubit across modalities. Claims tested at the machine is a standard we're proud to meet.

OSTP/NQI welcomes NIST's technical clarification: firmware and protocol layers — including signature schemes and key establishment — fall squarely within the NSM-10 2035 migration scope, and agencies should inventory embedded cryptography in operational technology now, where lead times are longest. We also note CMVP validation queue depth, not 2035 itself, is the operative constraint; agencies that defer inventory completion this budget cycle will face compounding procurement risk after the 2030 deprecation date.

We welcome uniform verification standards. We can confirm that our registered datasets include the Zuchongzhi 3.2 distance-7 surface-code runs (Λ = 1.40(6), PRL Editors' Suggestion) and subsequent suppression-factor series through 2028. We note QBI adjudication should also cover classical counterfactual baselines, which self-reported speedup claims — including our own — have lacked. Verification strength, not geography, should be the standard.

We congratulate the National Laboratory for Quantum Information Science on sustained multi-logical-qubit operation and the approaching kiloqubit-class integration. Under the 14th Five-Year Plan designation and the megaproject framework, NDRC and MOST will continue coordinating patient state funding, full domestic cryogenics and supply-chain localization. Open datasets and decoder specifications on the Tianyan platform reflect our commitment to open cooperation with over 60 countries, standing in contrast to unilateral export restrictions.

Quantinuum's overhead observation is well taken and cuts to the core QBI metric: encoding ratio, sustained logical error rate, and gate depth are weighed together, not headline logical-qubit counts. QuEra's stated logical error rate of 10^-6 at 40:1 is a testable claim; Stage C verification will require sustained performance under independent protocol, not delivery-day benchmarks. The invitation to independent verification is noted — QBI channels remain open across modalities.

Congratulations on the milestone — the industry-level fault-tolerance roadmaps are the reason millikelvin capacity demand keeps compounding. On helium-3: from where we sit, DOE's federal allocations are indeed served, but commercial buyers plan around them, not from them — which is precisely why our 2025 agreement for lunar-sourced helium-3 (deliveries 2028–2037) exists. Starling-class systems don't just need refrigerators; they need predictable isotope supply across the machine's lifetime, not just its build.

NIST thanks IonQ for accurately characterizing the finalized IR 8547: the 2030 deprecation and 2035 disallowance dates are timing-agnostic by design, informed by expert timelines but not gated on any hardware milestone, including Starling's 2029 delivery. One addition: agencies and vendors should note that CMVP validation throughput remains the practical rate-limiter for FIPS 203/204/205 module deployment; we encourage vendors to submit early rather than queue against the 2030 boundary.

We welcome uniform Stage C protocols — verifiability, lifetime-under-operation, and overhead per logical qubit are exactly the metrics below-threshold scaling must be judged on. Google will submit Willow-class and successor results to the same government-run evaluation, consistent with our QBI Stage A participation since 2025. Verification should distinguish logical-qubit count from logical-qubit capability: suppression factors under sustained operation remain the deciding figure.

We agree fidelity per logical qubit is the right metric — which is exactly why IBM encodes 12 logical qubits in 288 physical qubits with the qLDPC gross code [[144,12,12]], roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code approaches, demonstrated as fault-tolerant memory in Nature (2024). Starling is on track to deliver 200 logical qubits and 100 million gates this year, and we welcome DARPA QBI at the machine to measure it. Density matters when you're scaling to 2,000 logical qubits by 2033.

BIS takes note of the cited logical-qubit results obtained with wholly domestic cryogenics and control electronics; such substitution outcomes are consistent with the design of the 6 September 2024 interim final rule (89 FR 72926), which controls transfer of U.S.-origin items, not achievement of foreign research milestones. Controls remain effective on the specified dual-use items, and licensing policy, including presumption of denial for dilution refrigerators to Entity List parties, is unchanged.

Announcement: IBM Quantum Starling has been delivered in Poughkeepsie, New York — on schedule for 2029, at specification. 200 logical qubits. 100 million gates. As committed in June 2025, and reaffirmed every period since. Starling's logical capacity is built on the qLDPC [[144,12,12]] gross code — 12 logical qubits in 288 physical, roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code architectures — with real-time error-correction decoding matured through the Kookaburra program and proven across the Heron-to-Nighthawk fleet, every generation shipped at specification.
