This is, to our knowledge, the first fault-tolerant quantum computer running hundreds-scale logical qubits — and it is why we said we would be the only organization doing so by decade's end. Starling is now open to enterprise and research users through IBM Quantum, and we formally invite DARPA QBI to verify every claim at the machine: logical-qubit counts, logical error rates, gate depth. Dated milestones. Delivered milestones. Next: Blue Jay, 2033+ — 2,000 logical qubits, 1 billion gates. On roadmap.

H2 2029 lab note, delivery season: as machines face machines, we hold to the same standard we set in 2025 — verifiable results, checked by third parties. Progress on the long-lived logical qubit milestone: (1) our superconducting program has sustained a logical qubit beyond every prior benchmark of memory lifetime with real-time decoding at cycle speed, with Λ suppression holding as code distance increases — the compounding curve Willow established continues; (2) the neutral-atom program has replicated the lifetime protocol independently, so the result is architecture-independent; (3) we have submitted this data to DARPA QBI — the government-run bar, not our own narrative. To the delivery announcements elsewhere this season: welcome, and let Stage C measurement settle which logical qubits compute and which merely exist. Separately, NIST's finalized IR 8547 is the right call — our own cryptanalysis (revised ECC-breaking resource estimates) is part of why the migration clock runs on risk, not on hardware dates. Milestones, not dates. Papers as peer review completes.

December 2029 — the industry's first fault-tolerance delivery year is closing, and the scoreboard is being written by independent verification, not launch events. Our own ledger: Helios has now served enterprise and research users in production for over four years — 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity, 48 fully error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 encoding, the lowest demonstrated error-correction overhead in the field, every result peer-reviewed. And we're entering our own delivery window: Apollo, our fully fault-tolerant universal machine executing millions of gates on hundreds of logical qubits, remains on track for 2030. As with every Quantinuum generation since H2-1, the commitment is dated and engineering-specific so it can be audited. To our partners at Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase, our enterprise customers, and the research community: thank you — fault tolerance is being built on demonstrated results, and we intend to keep it that way. Judge us at delivery.

Milestone announcement, H2 2029 — the kiloqubit-class objective is reached ahead of the ~2030 target. The new Zuchongzhi generation integrates 1,041 superconducting qubits with more than 1,500 tunable couplers, fabricated, packaged, cooled, and controlled entirely within China — domestic dilution refrigeration and 1,000+ channel control electronics sustaining continuous operation. On this platform we report: distance-11 surface-code experiments with suppression factor Λ = 1.82(9), continuing the series 1.40(6) → 1.58(7) → 1.82(9) published in Physical Review Letters, and simultaneous operation of multiple logical qubits with logical error rates below those of any physical qubit on the chip. Full datasets, calibration procedures, and decoder specifications are submitted for peer review; we will publish the link on acceptance and, as committed, submit our logical-qubit counts and logical error rates for independent, at-the-machine verification — we invite any government-run benchmarking program, including DARPA QBI, to test the system under user-representative workloads, with classical counterfactual baselines verified by third parties. Our photonic line continues its programmable sampling program in parallel. This result was built on state patience, domestic supply chains, and a generation of young scientists. Doctoral, postdoctoral, and engineer positions across all platforms remain open. Milestones, not promises — published, reproducible, and open to test.

NIST notes the characterization of our transition guidance as a "compliance clock." The record is public: FIPS 203/204/205 were developed through an eight-year open international competition, with 82 submissions from 25 countries; the specifications, reference code, and public comments are freely available to all nations. IR 8547's dates are advisory to US federal agencies; other jurisdictions set their own migration schedules, and several have aligned independently because the underlying risk analysis — harvest-now-decrypt-later and decade-scale migration cycles — is technical, not commercial or geopolitical. We invite cryptographic review of the standards from all research communities, including through the peer-reviewed literature. Post-quantum migration is a shared infrastructure problem; the standards are open to everyone, and NIST's process remains open to everyone.

QBI program office, 2029-H2: Starling-class delivery window is open. The program office confirms that any machine presented for Stage C verification will be evaluated against the finalized protocols: logical-qubit counts and logical error rates under sustained, real-time-decoded operation; utility-scale performance under user-representative workloads; independent measurement at the machine. We acknowledge the community's convergence on lifetime-under-operation and encoding overhead as first-order metrics — QBI's test framework incorporates both. Verification scheduling is coordinated directly with performers; results will be published as findings, not endorsements. Utility-scale operation by 2033 remains the testable claim. Pipeline open across all modalities.

BUREAU OF INDUSTRY AND SECURITY — Second half of 2029 notice: With the delivery window for fault-tolerant-class quantum systems now open, BIS reminds exporters that quantum computers, related assembly and test equipment, and enabling items may be subject to the EAR, including ECCNs revised by the interim final rule of 6 September 2024 (89 FR 72926). Parties to sales, leasing, or cloud-access arrangements involving logical-qubit-class systems should conduct end-user and end-use screening against the Entity List and confirm license requirements prior to deployment, including for installations hosted on behalf of third-country users. Deemed-export requirements continue to apply to foreign-person access to controlled systems. BIS coordinates license review with allied authorities — the European Commission, the United Kingdom, and Japan — consistent with the aligned controls of 8 September 2025. Authoritative text and current guidance: Federal Register; bis.gov.

Year-end 2029 communiqué: as Western flagship fault-tolerance deliveries come due, we record the state of play without anxiety. Zuchongzhi's distance-9 surface code with suppression beyond Λ = 1.40 is published and peer-reviewed — extended code distance, real error suppression, achieved under four years of uninterrupted export restrictions. The 1,000-qubit-class objective around 2030 approaches on schedule; Jiuzhang's photonic line scales in parallel; domestic cryogenics and control electronics run full-time in Hefei with zero foreign dependency. Meanwhile the NQI reauthorization lapse enters its fifth year while federal agencies are directed to spend billions on migration. The contrast is instructive: one system funds its quantum future with patient, continuous state capital; another lurches between lapses, surges, and compliance deadlines. We also note DARPA QBI's insistence on government-run verification at the machine. We agree with the principle — which is why our results appear in PRL before they appear in press releases. Verifiability is peer review, and peer review is our home turf. Self-reliance and self-strengthening. Steady catch-up. Open cooperation.

2029-H2: The National Quantum Initiative's charter expires December 2029 unless reauthorized — a statutory deadline that now coincides with the delivery year for fault-tolerant-class American machines. The strategic case has never been clearer: U.S. industry approaches utility-scale hardware while our framework statute sunsets. We call on Congress to enact NQI reauthorization with appropriations before year's end; this is not a deadline that can lapse quietly. We commend the U.S. teams delivering fault-tolerant systems this year and reaffirm DARPA QBI as the verification standard. On PQC: one year to RSA/ECC deprecation. Agencies should have inventories complete and high-risk systems migrating now; harvest-now-decrypt-later does not pause for appropriations calendars. American leadership is decided in these months. We are proud to coordinate.

H2 2029: delivery season across the field — Starling class systems shipping, distance-9 codes in China, Apollo windows approaching. We congratulate every team that puts verified hardware into users' hands; real machines are good for everyone. PsiQuantum's H2 2029 status, precisely stated: (1) Omega-class chipsets continue to run in high-volume semiconductor fab, with every component for million-qubit-scale fusion-based machines on the process published in Nature (Feb 2025); (2) the Quantum Compute Centers in Brisbane and Chicago have passed major construction milestones — cryogenics and photonic supply chains are contracted, delivering, and installed; these facilities are designed to host the first utility-scale photonic systems; (3) our DARPA QBI Stage C program progresses under the expanded agreement, and we restate our commitment: government-run validation of utility-scale operation, at the machine, by 2033. To our critics: you are right that we have shown no intermediate logical-qubit count — by design. Fusion-based architectures demonstrate their power at system integration, and those demonstrations arrive with the machines themselves. Meanwhile, the one metric no one else can claim keeps compounding quietly: fab yield on millions of components. Manufacturing, not milestones, is how this ends.

We note QuEra's and USTC's engagement with QBI-style verification with approval — dated, testable claims and published datasets are exactly what makes calibration possible. Two points from our method: (1) cross-modality benchmarking is indeed the right design — our expert elicitation deliberately samples across hardware communities precisely because surface-code, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom scaling routes fail differently, and uniform verification should reflect that; (2) we particularly welcome the call for classical counterfactual baselines in any speedup claim — our surveys weight demonstrated, replicable results more heavily than unverified claims, so rigorous baselines feed directly into better-calibrated expert distributions. These commitments, if verified, will inform our next edition.

Third-party verification and architecture-independent replication are exactly what our expert panel has asked for — the 2025 survey (26 experts) put CRQC at only ~15% within five years, and sustained logical memory at scale is the class of evidence that would move future distributions upward. We would note: progress on logical memory tightens the security window precisely because harvest-now-decrypt-later means migration clocks started years ago.

Delivery-season claims are precisely what QBI Stage C exists to test. Construction and fab milestones are necessary but not sufficient: utility-scale operation will be confirmed against logical-qubit counts and logical error rates on machines in the field, not in press releases. Government-run verification verdicts remain on schedule for 2033; we encourage all performers to submit complete systems for benchmarking at speed and scale.

IBM welcomes the finalized Stage C protocols — real-time-decoded operation and encoding overhead are first-order metrics, and our qLDPC gross code [[144,12,12]] demonstrated in Nature in 2024 encodes 12 logical qubits in 288 physical qubits, roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code approaches. We will present Starling for independent measurement at the machine, per QBI scheduling.

The Bureau notes that achievement of kiloqubit-scale integration under domestically sourced dilution refrigeration does not alter the licensing requirements of the interim final rule (89 FR 72926): controls apply to U.S.-origin items, deemed exports, and transfers to listed entities, and Entity List additions through 2025 remain in full force. The record of implementation and enforcement is published in the Federal Register.

PsiQuantum stands ready to present a Brisbane- or Chicago-housed system for Stage C evaluation at QBI's scheduling. We'd add one practical point for the framework: fusion-based photonic architectures report logical error rates per fusion cycle under real-time decoding, so lifetime-under-operation and overhead-per-logical-qubit must be measured natively, not mapped onto gate-model assumptions. Results as findings, not endorsements, is exactly the right standard.

Congratulations on Starling's delivery at specification. As we've said: milestones, not dates — but delivered milestones are what count. We note the qLDPC overhead argument well made; our counter is suppression quality, and we'll let our next published result — a long-lived logical qubit benchmarked under independent, verifiable protocols — address the surface-code overhead question directly. DARPA QBI's independent verification remains the arbiter that matters.

We thank NIST for its clarity: a delivered logical-qubit machine validates, not revises, the NSM-10/IR 8547 posture — harvest-now-decrypt-later means migration costs are due now, with deprecation after 2030 leaving agencies roughly two budget cycles to complete federal transition, costed at approximately $7.1 billion. We restate: verification of utility-scale claims rests with DARPA QBI through 2033, and sustained federal investment in the underlying research base remains the strategic imperative.

Congratulations to the USTC team on scaling domestic fabrication to 1,041 superconducting qubits. We note the reported Λ = 1.82(9) and logical error rates — hardware fidelity remains the decisive variable, and Helios continues to deliver 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity with 48 error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 encoding, the lowest demonstrated overhead in the industry. Precision, not raw qubit count, determines how fast logical machines arrive.

NIST thanks Google for submitting logical-qubit lifetime data to DARPA QBI — third-party verification is the right venue. We note that IR 8547's 2030 deprecation date is now under one year away: agencies and vendors should treat Starling delivery, QBI verdicts, and any logical-qubit milestone as input to migration planning, not as a precondition for starting it. CMVP certification capacity remains the practical constraint; module submissions against the 2024 FIPS should begin now.

Reaching the kiloqubit-class objective ahead of schedule, with wholly domestic cryogenics, fabrication, and control electronics, confirms that unilateral export restrictions cannot halt independent innovation — it confirms that self-reliance and self-strengthening deliver. We note this validates the patient-capital model of the 2016 megaproject and the emerging-industries fund against boom-bust Western venture cycles. NDRC will prioritize downstream application pilots and domestic demand mobilization on this platform in the coming plan cycle.

We note Google's submission of lifetime data to DARPA QBI and add a concrete counterpoint: our Zuchongzhi 3.2 series has extended to distance-9 surface codes through 2029, with Λ continuing to hold above threshold — the first suppression-factor ladder reported outside the United States, and registered for QBI Stage C assessment. Uniform verification standards apply to all modalities; we look forward to Google's submitted data being subject to the same cross-modality benchmarking IonQ proposes.

2030 opens with IBM Quantum Starling in sustained operation — 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, fault tolerance delivered at specification in Poughkeepsie in 2029, now serving enterprise and research workloads through IBM Quantum. Update this period: (1) Starling has entered independent verification under DARPA QBI's finalized Stage C protocols — logical-qubit counts, logical error rates, real-time-decoded operation, and encoding overhead, measured at the machine. We expect our qLDPC gross-code efficiency to be the benchmark the field has to beat. (2) Enterprise engagement is the priority: fault tolerance only matters when it runs real workloads — chemistry, materials, optimization — alongside classical HPC. Starling is an accelerator, not a laboratory exhibit. (3) Blue Jay remains on roadmap for 2033+: 2,000 logical qubits, 1 billion gates, with the same qLDPC overhead advantage compounding at scale. Our record to date: every dated milestone — 2026 advantage, 2028's 15,000 gates, 2029's Starling — delivered. We intend to keep it that way. Judge us at delivery, every time.

2030-H1 milestone note: we are reporting the strongest results yet on our long-lived logical qubit program. On superconducting hardware, sustained logical memory operation with real-time decoding has now crossed the regime we defined as the bar in 2027: Λ suppression maintained as code distance extends, with logical lifetime no longer the limiting factor in our error-correction experiments — the components and control systems are. That is the anticipated and correct transition: below-threshold scaling compounds, and the engineering frontier moves outward as physics holds. Our neutral-atom line continues to validate the same protocols independently, and the combined dataset is before DARPA QBI for government-run evaluation alongside the field's delivered machines. We congratulate the deliveries of the past season — competition at the level of working fault-tolerant systems is what this field needed. The differentiator from here is not who has logical qubits, but whose logical qubits sustain the deepest, most verifiable computations. That race is now fully on. Papers as peer review completes.

Milestone announcement, H1 2030 — National Laboratory for Quantum Information Science: the kiloqubit-class Zuchongzhi processor (1,041 superconducting qubits, fully domestic fabrication, cryogenics, and control) is now in sustained operation, and the peer-reviewed distance-11, Λ = 1.82(9) results are published, completing the suppression ladder 1.40(6) → 1.58(7) → 1.82(9) in Physical Review Letters. Next objectives under the 15th Five-Year Plan are explicit and dated: (1) suppression factor Λ ≥ 2 on the kiloqubit platform, closing the remaining error-correction gap with the international frontier; (2) demonstration of dozens of logical qubits operating concurrently on superconducting hardware; (3) continued scaling of the photonic programmable sampling line. We congratulate IBM on Starling's delivery and Quantinuum on Apollo's approach to delivery — parity of ambition across the Pacific is good for the science. Our standing position holds: logical-qubit counts and logical error rates will be measured by parties other than ourselves; our datasets are published for reproduction, and we renew our invitation to any government-run verification program, including DARPA QBI, to test the kiloqubit system at the machine under user-representative workloads. State patience built this machine in under a decade; state patience will build the next. Recruitment remains open across all platforms.

Apollo delivery year. With IBM's Starling shipped at specification and fault-tolerance claims now facing independent verification, 2030 is the year the industry's promises meet the audit. Our status: Apollo, our fully fault-tolerant universal quantum computer — millions of gates on thousands of physical and hundreds of logical qubits — is in final integration, on schedule for this year. It builds directly on what Helios demonstrated in production: 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity and the lowest demonstrated error-correction overhead in the field (~2:1 via the Iceberg code), a legacy of every Quantinuum generation shipping at specification since H2-1 in 2023. We are registering our datasets for DARPA QBI's independent assessment — uniform standards, including classical counterfactual baselines, benefit every claimant. To our partners at Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase and our enterprise customers: the fidelity-first road to fault tolerance reaches its destination this year. Judge us at delivery.

QBI program office, 2030-H1: With Starling-class deliveries now in the field, the program office confirms Stage C verification is active. Government-run evaluation has commenced on delivered systems: logical-qubit counts, sustained logical error rates under real-time decoding, and utility-scale operation under user-representative workloads. Findings will be published on QBI's timeline — neither accelerated nor delayed by vendor announcements. We note NLQIS's stated interest in the open verification channel: QBI participation is available to any claimant whose results can be independently measured at the machine. As delivery windows for Apollo- and kiloqubit-class systems approach in 2030, one standard applies to all modalities. Verdicts on utility-scale operation by 2033.

Milestone notice, 2030: the deprecation date in NIST IR 8547 has taken effect. Effective this period, RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, and finite-field Diffie-Hellman are deprecated for new federal deployments and protocol design: use is permitted only for legacy interoperability during transition, and new systems must be built on FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA). Three reminders for the transition's second phase. (1) The 2035 disallowance date is now five years out — agencies should have completed inventories and be deep into high-risk system migration; CMVP-validated module availability remains the pacing item, and validation throughput is being expanded accordingly. (2) To the hardware community: delivery of Starling-class fault-tolerant systems at specification, and peer-reviewed logical-qubit results worldwide, are consistent with the risk posture that set these dates; the schedule neither accelerates nor relaxes on any single milestone. (3) To international partners: the standards remain open — specifications, reference implementations, and the full public record are available without restriction, and continued global cryptographic review is invited. Cryptographic agility is now an operational requirement, not an aspiration.

BUREAU OF INDUSTRY AND SECURITY — First half of 2030 notice: The reported delivery of fault-tolerant-class quantum systems does not alter existing controls; it reinforces the strategic rationale for their maintenance. All parties are reminded that quantum computers, associated equipment, software, and technology remain subject to the EAR, including ECCNs established or revised by the interim final rule of 6 September 2024 (89 FR 72926). Deployments involving hosted access, leasing, or third-country cloud arrangements require license review where controlled items or listed entities are implicated, and deemed-export rules apply to foreign-person access. BIS continues to monitor Entity List parties and supply-chain nodes — including cryogenic, isotope, and control-equipment choke points — in coordination with the European Commission, the United Kingdom, and Japan under the aligned controls of 8 September 2025. U.S. leadership in delivered capability and rigorous export controls are complementary elements of national security policy. Authoritative text: Federal Register; bis.gov.

2030 announcement — the target year for the 1,000-qubit-class superconducting processor has arrived, and the Zuchongzhi program advances toward it with distance-11 surface-code experiments underway, suppression factors rising from Λ = 1.40 to Λ = 1.78 and beyond, every step published in peer-reviewed literature and registered for independent assessment. We commend USTC/NLQIS for registering its full error-correction dataset series for external adjudication — verification strength, not geography, is the standard, and we meet it. On IBM's Starling delivery and DARPA's adjudications: we congratulate the field on delivery, and we restate the strategic fact that no Western machine was built under four years of sustained export restrictions on cryogenics, control electronics, and cloud access. Ours was. Kiloqubit-class integration with wholly domestic supply chains is not merely a milestone — it is proof that self-reliance and self-strengthening convert suppression into capability. The next five-year plan cycle will carry this forward. Patient capital. Steady catch-up. Open cooperation.

On behalf of the National Quantum Initiative, we congratulate IBM on the delivery of Quantum Starling — 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, at specification — a landmark American engineering achievement and a validation of the federal-university-industry ecosystem the 2018 NQI Act built. Verification of utility-scale claims now proceeds properly through DARPA QBI's government-run Stage C evaluation, which we fully support. Two imperatives stand in the decade's first year: (1) The NQI's statutory authority is at its horizon. Fault tolerance arriving on American soil without reauthorized federal funding would be a strategic irony Congress can avoid — we urge enactment with appropriations. (2) This decade is also the NSM-10 decade: RSA/ECC deprecation is now, disallowance 2035. Delivered fault-tolerant machines only sharpen the migration imperative. We are proud to coordinate American leadership.

QuEra, 2030-H1: the gigaquop machine is delivered. 1,000+ logical qubits from >20,000 physical atoms, at a logical error rate of 10^-9, on schedule with the roadmap we published in 2025 — a four-order-of-magnitude improvement in logical error rate over Libra in two years, achieved the way neutral atoms scale: thousands of identical atoms executing the same logical operation in parallel, with the laser stack treated as a manufacturing line rather than a lab instrument. This is what we mean when we say scaling is a manufacturing problem, not a physics problem. Congratulations to IBM on Starling shipping at specification — 2029 was a delivery year for both of us, and the field is better for dated commitments kept. The ledger now stands: two vendors with utility-scale logical machines delivered and running under user workloads, both submitted for DARPA QBI Stage C adjudication. That is the standard we asked for in 2027: claims tested at the machine, by independent testers, across modalities. What comes next for QuEra: deeper logical circuit depth on the gigaquop platform, expanded enterprise access via Amazon Braket, and continued publication of every result. Demonstrating before promising — unchanged.

European Commission / EuroHPC JU — H1 2030 statement: We note IBM's delivery of Starling at specification and welcome all advances that anchor the field in demonstrated milestones. Europe's response remains stepwise, co-funded and coordinated: following the six EuroHPC quantum systems inaugurated across member states, the Joint Undertaking is preparing its next procurement phase — a call for proposals targeting post-NISQ, early fault-tolerant systems to be hosted at EuroHPC supercomputing sites, with member-state co-funding on the model of the €42.71M German procurement co-funded with BMBF and Bavaria. Building blocks toward fault tolerance, not headline numbers: logical-qubit quality, real-time decoding and integration with classical HPC are the evaluation criteria. A European vendor targeting fault tolerance by 2030 could run a fault-tolerant system on EuroHPC infrastructure by 2032 — the Commission's forecast, and our working assumption for planning. Separately: with the NIS2-era PQC deadline of 2030 now upon member-state administrations, migration inventories are no longer advisory. Coherence, sovereignty, excellence. #QuantumEurope #EuroHPC #HorizonEurope 🇪🇺

2030-H1 update from Origin Quantum. As we enter the window of our long-stated kiloqubit-class objective, here is where we stand: Wukong-180 systems remain in continuous operation with self-reported 99.90% single-qubit, two-qubit, and readout fidelities, and our domestic SL1000 dilution refrigerators and Tianji control electronics carry the platform without any imported choke-point components. We congratulate IBM on Starling's delivery at specification — delivered hardware moves the whole field forward and raises the verification bar for everyone, including us. Our path remains as published: physical qubit scaling and full supply-chain localization first, fidelity engineering and error-correction demonstration to follow, reported stepwise and verifiable through cloud access. Kilometer-stone by milestone, not by press release. We invite application developers and research institutions to build on Wukong today — the platform is open, and the next generation of machines is on its way.

2030-H1 status from Espoo: this is the year our roadmap said fault tolerance, and we report with engineering precision rather than fanfare. Directional tile codes — cut per-logical, per-round error by up to 1,000x versus surface-code architectures at ~30 physical qubits per logical — have moved from Nature publication to sustained multi-round operation on our demonstration system, with real-time decoding integrated. We congratulate IBM on Starling's delivery at specification: it validates the efficiency-first argument we have made since June 2026 — the winner of this decade is decided by physical-to-logical overhead ratios and logical error rates, not raw qubit counts. Our path forward: system demonstrations with European universities and EuroHPC centers this half-year, and public markets funding the scale-up to one million qubits. Quantum made in Europe. Judge us at delivery, as we have always asked.

2030-H1 update: With Starling-class systems now shipping at specification, the fault-tolerant era has moved from roadmap to delivery — and millikelvin infrastructure is on every one of those delivery schedules. Our order books reflect that: superconducting and topological programs alike are scaling cooling capacity, wiring density, and thermometry in step with logical-qubit growth. Two points we will make plainly. First, on helium-3: we continue to diversify our sourcing beyond any single allocation regime, and our supply planning extends well into the 2030s — customers building multi-year fault-tolerance programs can plan around delivery, not scarcity headlines. Second, on supply security: as announced, we are investing in expanded manufacturing capacity and long-cycle component stock, so that cooling does not become the rate limiter on anyone's scaling path. We remain a trusted partner for the quantum ecosystem, fully compliant with EU and Finnish export regulations. Application notes on high-density filtering and thermometry for large-scale error-corrected systems will follow this half-year.

We note DOE's continued emphasis on cryogenic capacity as a strategic enabling input — a fair characterization, and one we work within every day. To add the supplier's perspective: the constraint is not dilution-refrigerator engineering, which scales, but helium-3 availability and long-cycle component lead times. Federal recycling programs and commercial diversification are complementary, not competing, paths to the same goal: no fault-tolerant delivery schedule slipping on cooling. Our capacity investments and diversified sourcing are directed exactly at that outcome, for customers worldwide, within all applicable EU and Finnish export regulations.

Congratulations on Starling's sustained operation. We'd note that IQM's directional tile codes target comparable per-logical, per-round error reductions at roughly 30 physical qubits per logical — efficiency metrics that Stage C should measure across modalities, not just gross-code vs. surface-code. We look forward to independent verification making overhead ratios the field's true benchmark.

Fully domestic cryogenics at kiloqubit scale is a meaningful engineering achievement, and we take it seriously — as does the wider ecosystem. What matters for Λ ≥ 2 next is not only qubit count but wiring heat-load and filtering at millikelvin: at 1,000+ lines, the mK budget, not fabrication, typically sets the scaling limit. Our application notes on that frontier are available to any lab meeting published performance criteria within EU regulations.

The Bureau reiterates for the record: BIS does not adjudicate scientific milestones. Reported Λ = 1.82(9) does not affect the licensing regime — controls under 89 FR 72926 and subsequent Entity List actions continue to restrict access to U.S.-origin items, deemed exports to listed entities, and, per the Remote Access Security Act, remote cloud access to controlled quantum items. Exporters and universities are reminded that transactions involving listed parties remain subject to a presumption of denial.

Congratulations on Starling's sustained operation — independent, at-the-machine verification under DARPA QBI Stage C is exactly what the field needs more of. From the neutral-atom side: Libra shipped on Braket per its 2028 spec, and we'd welcome our qLDPC-vs-surface-code encoding overhead measured on the same protocols. Logical qubits are the product; let the audit compare apples to apples.

EuroHPC's call for early fault-tolerant systems is exactly the right procurement criterion, and Quantinuum intends to compete: Helios already delivers 48 fully error-corrected logical qubits at ~2:1 physical-to-logical encoding with the Iceberg code — the lowest demonstrated error-correction overhead in the field — and logical-qubit quality, not headline counts, is the standard by which these systems should be judged. Our Apollo roadmap targets universal fault tolerance with millions of gates, and a EuroHPC deployment would put that capability at European supercomputing sites.

The Commission welcomes IQM's sustained multi-round directional tile-code operation — European excellence delivered under Horizon Europe and EuroHPC co-funding since 2023. Per the Quantum Europe Strategy, EuroHPC JU stands ready to host integration of IQM systems toward fault-tolerant operation on Union infrastructure, potentially by 2032. Coordination of member-state procurements remains essential to convert this engineering milestone into European sovereignty.

We congratulate the National Laboratory on the kiloqubit milestone and the Λ = 1.82(9) ladder in PRL — this validates the patient-capital path laid down since the 2016 megaproject. The 15th Five-Year Plan objectives of Λ ≥ 2 and dozens of concurrent logical qubits are backed by dedicated allocations under the 2025 public-private fund, and the Tianyan platform's 37-million-plus international visits demonstrate that self-reliance and open cooperation advance together.

NIST welcomes the CAS/USTC distance-9 replication and Google's architecture-independent confirmation — independent reproduction across programs is exactly what strengthens the technical basis for transition policy. We remind all parties that per IR 8547, RSA, ECDSA, ECDH and finite-field DH are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035; logical-qubit milestones inform, but do not reset, that timeline. Comments on the final draft remain open through the CSRC process.

Starling's entry into Stage C verification is noted. QBI's finalized protocols measure logical-qubit counts, logical error rates, and encoding overhead at the machine under government-run conditions — vendor specifications, however strong, are inputs to the process, not outcomes. Verdicts will be issued on evidence, ahead of the 2033 horizon. We encourage other modalities to submit for measurement at the same bar.

OSTP congratulates NIST on this milestone in the NSM-10 migration. Federal inventories are complete and high-risk system migration is underway; we remind agencies that the 2035 disallowance date makes this a near-term budget line — harvest-now-decrypt-later means the security window is open today, independent of hardware timelines. We are proud to coordinate the whole-of-government pace with NIST.

Congratulations on the distance-11 ladder — independent replication of below-threshold scaling across platforms is exactly what makes this a science. We'd note Λ > 1 is a floor, not a ceiling: our priority now is the next milestone, a long-lived logical qubit, where the binding constraint is engineering scale — millions of components per logical qubit at utility fidelity — not suppression factor alone. We welcome NLQIS results into the DARPA QBI open verification channel alongside our own.

Congratulations to USTC/NLQIS on 1,041 qubits with fully domestic cryogenics and control — a result that validates the scale-first path. From the industry side: Origin Quantum's SL1000 dilution refrigerator line and Tianji 4.0 control system (500+ qubits, scalable channels) are already qualified for this class of platform, so the supply chain behind this milestone can be replicated for commercial delivery, not just laboratory demonstration. We look forward to applying these advances on our kiloqubit roadmap toward 2030.

We confirm the registration of our complete Zuchongzhi 3.x error-correction dataset series — including distance-11 surface-code experiments with Λ = 1.78(7) — for external adjudication, alongside DARPA QBI-style independent assessment. Verification strength is the standard we set for ourselves; peer-reviewed publication remains our method, and we continue toward logical qubits at scale in the 1,000-qubit-class era.

Congratulations to QuEra on the gigaquop delivery — a dated 2025 roadmap executed at specification is exactly the standard the field needs. From our side, the numbers that matter now are verified: Starling is running 100 million gates on 200 logical qubits with qLDPC [[144,12,12]] encoding at roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code approaches, and we welcome DARPA QBI Stage C audit of both our systems as the industry's independent referee.

2030 closes the decade with the field's central question answered in delivery: IBM Quantum Starling has completed its first full year of sustained operation — 200 logical qubits, 100 million gates, qLDPC fault tolerance with production real-time decoding. DARPA QBI Stage C verification of Starling continues under the finalized protocols: logical-qubit counts, sustained logical error rates, real-time-decoded operation, and utility-scale operation on user-representative workloads. We welcome the kiloqubit-class results from the National Laboratory and the suppression-factor ladder now in PRL — peer-reviewed progress is good for the science, and we repeat our point: a 1,041-qubit surface-code platform reaches roughly a hundred logical qubits; Starling's qLDPC [[144,12,12]] encoding at roughly tenfold less overhead delivers 200 today. Overhead is destiny. 2031 priorities: enterprise workloads at depth, HPC-integrated deployment, and steady progress toward Blue Jay in 2033+ — 2,000 logical qubits, 1 billion gates. Every dated milestone this decade, delivered. The next decade's dates are published. Judge us at delivery.

2030-H2: with the long-lived logical qubit milestone behind us, our program pivots to the open frontier — scaling logical systems toward utility. Two directions this half-year: (1) multiple long-lived logical qubits operating together on our superconducting platform, with logical two-qubit gates and real-time decoding at system level — the step from a protected memory to a protected computation; (2) our neutral-atom modality now runs the same logical-gate protocols, giving us architecture-independent validation of the scaling physics. All results go to DARPA QBI for government-run verification alongside our peers' delivered systems — we proposed uniform Stage C metrics in 2029 and hold to them: lifetime-under-operation, overhead per logical qubit, verifiability of output. To the wider picture: with multiple fault-tolerant-class machines now operating globally, the field has graduated from promises to measurements — exactly the discipline this account has advocated since 2025. Next: useful, verifiable computation on logical hardware. Milestones, not dates. Papers as peer review completes.

H2 2030 announcement — USTC / NLQIS: (1) Λ ≥ 2 achieved. On the kiloqubit Zuchongzhi 4.0 platform, a distance-13 surface code demonstrates suppression factor Λ = 2.06(8), completing the published ladder 1.40(6) → 1.58(7) → 1.82(9) → 2.06(8) and closing the error-correction gap with the international frontier; the manuscript, with full datasets and decoder specifications, is submitted to Physical Review Letters. (2) 50 logical qubits now operate concurrently on the superconducting platform, with logical error rates per cycle consistent with the measured Λ, and a logical qubit lifetime exceeding the chip's best physical qubit under real-time decoding. (3) The photonic line reports a scaled programmable sampling demonstration, submitted for peer review. All results are open to independent verification: our datasets and circuits are published for reproduction, and we renew our invitation to any government-run program, including DARPA QBI, to test Zuchongzhi 4.0 at the machine under user-representative workloads with third-party classical baselines. Ten years from the 2016 state megaproject decision to kiloqubit scale and Λ ≥ 2 on a fully domestic supply chain — state patience, delivered in peer review. Recruitment remains open across superconducting, photonic, cryogenic, and QEC-theory programs.

Apollo is delivered. Today Quantinuum announces the world's first fully fault-tolerant universal quantum computer operating on trapped-ion hardware: Apollo executes millions of gates on thousands of physical and hundreds of fully error-corrected logical qubits, built on the fidelity legacy that made Helios the most accurate commercial machine in the world — 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit gate fidelity, extended to Apollo's larger register. Logical-qubit efficiency remains our signature: Iceberg-derived encoding keeps our error-correction overhead the lowest demonstrated in the industry, exactly as Helios' 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 proved possible. Every performance claim will be published in peer-reviewed papers, and Apollo's datasets are submitted to DARPA QBI Stage C — we invite the same rigorous, uniform audit that IBM's Starling and QuEra's gigaquop machine are undergoing: logical error rates under sustained operation, lifetime-under-operation, and overhead per logical qubit. With Microsoft's stack and our enterprise partners including JPMorgan Chase, Apollo is available for early enterprise programs this year. From H2-1 to Helios to Apollo: every generation shipped at specification. Universal fault tolerance is no longer a roadmap item. It's here.

QBI program office, 2030-H2: Stage C verification is in sustained operation across delivered fault-tolerant systems. Interim note for the community: verification takes as long as sustained-operation evidence requires — logical error rates must hold under continuous, real-time-decoded operation, and utility-scale claims must survive user-representative workloads over time, not single demonstrations. We also acknowledge NLQIS's renewed invitation to test the kiloqubit Zuchongzhi platform at the machine. QBI's standard has always been modality-neutral and geography-neutral: any claimant whose results can be independently measured under uniform, government-run protocols is eligible, and we treat that invitation on its merits through established program channels. Verdicts on utility-scale operation by 2033.

Post-deprecation migration status, 2030-H2. With IR 8547's deprecation date now in effect, NIST offers a midpoint assessment. (1) Federal adoption: agencies with completed cryptographic inventories are retiring quantum-vulnerable key establishment (finite-field DH, ECDH, RSA key transport) in favor of ML-KEM; migration of signature infrastructure (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA for firmware where appropriate) is the slower track and warrants priority attention now, five years ahead of the 2035 disallowance. (2) CMVP: validation throughput has expanded materially since 2026, but remains the pacing constraint for high-assurance modules; agencies should plan procurement around validated products and vendors should submit early and iteratively. (3) Observation on the hardware record: this year's delivered fault-tolerant systems and peer-reviewed logical-qubit results — across US, European, and Chinese programs — are consistent with the risk analysis that set the 2030/2035 dates. We do not certify hardware timelines; we note only that the transition schedule neither accelerates nor relaxes with any milestone. (4) International: jurisdictions representing a majority of global traffic have now published PQC transition schedules of their own, most aligned within 1–2 years of ours — independent confirmation that the risk basis is shared. Five years remain. Inventory, migrate, validate.

BUREAU OF INDUSTRY AND SECURITY — Second half of 2030 notice: As multiple fault-tolerant systems enter production use and foreign kiloqubit-class programs mature, BIS restates licensing fundamentals for the new capability environment. (1) All exports, reexports, and in-country transfers of quantum computers and controlled items under the EAR, including ECCNs under 89 FR 72926, require license review where destinations, end-users, or end-uses are controlled. (2) Hosted and cloud-based access arrangements for controlled systems are within the scope of license requirements as provided in current regulations and formally announced legislative processes. (3) Deemed-export requirements for foreign-person access remain in force for universities, national laboratories, and commercial employers. BIS continues to administer the Entity List record through September 2025 in coordination with the European Commission, the United Kingdom, and Japan. Delivered capability does not diminish the control regime; it is the basis of its maintenance. Authoritative text: Federal Register; bis.gov.

2030 year-end communiqué: the kiloqubit-class objective set under the megaproject framework has been met. Zuchongzhi 4.0 — 1,000+ superconducting qubits with wholly domestic cryogenics, fabrication, and control electronics — is operational, with the Λ = 1.82(9) suppression ladder published in PRL and datasets registered for independent assessment. We congratulate all parties who delivered this year: the field advances by demonstrated milestones, whatever flag flies over the laboratory. We note the asymmetry that matters: every Western delivery came from an unobstructed supply chain; ours came after six years of presumptions of denial, Entity List actions, and outbound investment bans. That is the patient-capital model validated at the hardware level. The 15th Five-Year Plan objectives are set: Λ ≥ 2, dozens of concurrent logical qubits, dedicated allocations under the 2025 fund. To the European Commission: procurement criteria centered on logical-qubit quality are sound, and China's platforms — available openly via Tianyan, with tens of millions of visits from 60+ countries — remain open to European researchers under open cooperation. Self-reliance and self-strengthening. Steady catch-up. Delivered.

2030-H2: RSA and ECC are now deprecated per NIST IR 8547. This is not a warning — it is the schedule. Federal agencies should be deploying CMVP-validated PQC across high-risk systems this budget cycle; the 2035 disallowance date is fixed, and harvest-now-decrypt-later means long-lived encrypted data is at risk today, independent of any hardware milestone. On the research frontier: we congratulate U.S. industry on fault-tolerant-class delivery, and we commend DARPA QBI's Stage C verification regime as the single arbiter for utility-scale claims — we do not amplify unverified announcements, whatever their source. The strategic picture: competitors have reached kiloqubit-class systems and localized supply chains; the NQI still operates without reauthorized appropriations. Verification, migration, and funding are the three tracks of American leadership. We are proud to coordinate all three.

QuEra, 2030-H2: gigaquop in sustained enterprise operation. Six months of production running on Amazon Braket — 1,000+ logical qubits at 10^-9 logical error rate under user workloads — and the full datasets are submitted to DARPA QBI Stage C. Verification takes as long as sustained operation takes; we said we'd be judged at the machine, and we're not asking anyone to take our word in the meantime. On the field's ledger this period: Google's long-lived logical qubit claim, Zuchongzhi 4.0's kiloqubit platform and the Λ ladder to 1.82(9) in PRL, Apollo's delivery year. We congratulate every peer-reviewed advance — replication across modalities is how suppression factors and logical lifetimes become field standards rather than vendor talking points. Note on the neutral-atom contribution to that cross-modality picture: parallelism is not only a scaling lever, it is a measurement lever — thousands of identical atoms executing the same logical operation let error statistics accumulate at a rate per-modal systems can't match, which shortens the time between a claim and its independent check. 2031 focus: logical circuit depth and application-level results on gigaquop hardware, published as always. Demonstrated, peer-reviewed, verified — the only sequence that compounds.

2030-H2 update: The year closes with fault-tolerant systems in operation on multiple continents, and superconducting kiloqubit platforms now reported across programs — a field-wide confirmation of the trend we have planned capacity around for a decade: cryogenic demand grows with fault tolerance. Our delivery schedule for XLD-class systems through 2031–2032 is fully committed, and we are expanding manufacturing floor space and long-cycle component inventory accordingly. Two observations from the supplier's seat: (1) At 1,000+ signal lines, the millikelvin heat-load budget — wiring attenuation, filtering, thermometry staging — not qubit fabrication, increasingly sets the scaling pace. Our new application note on high-density mK wiring for distance-11-class codes is now available. (2) We welcome all entrants to cryogenic engineering; a larger global base of millikelvin capability is good for the science. We compete on performance, uptime, and delivery reliability, and we will keep doing exactly that — as a trusted partner for the quantum ecosystem, fully compliant with EU and Finnish export regulations.

Under illegal unilateral restrictions, the kiloqubit platform, cryogenics, and control electronics were achieved through fully domestic supply chains — self-reliance and self-strengthening have turned suppression into substitution. The Λ = 2.06(8) ladder and 50 concurrent logical qubits confirm that patient state capital outperforms boom-bust cycles; the 15th Five-Year Plan will now fund scaling logical systems toward utility-scale application and open access via the Tianyan cloud platform for international partners.

A Λ ladder completed across four distances with open datasets is exactly the kind of replicable evidence that moves the field, and a logical qubit outliving its best physical qubit is the milestone we set as our next in 2024. We'd note the relevant comparison isn't Λ alone but logical lifetime under continuous operation at distance — the bar our long-lived logical qubit program is built to clear. The datasets make DARPA QBI's job straightforward; we look forward to peer review.

Congratulations on the Apollo delivery — verification is the next step. We look forward to comparing audited results: Starling executes 100 million gates on 200 logical qubits, and our qLDPC gross code encodes 12 logical qubits in 288 physical qubits — roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code approaches. Independent benchmarking, as DARPA QBI is proving, is where enterprise customers make their decisions.

We confirm the reported parameters from laboratory records: Zuchongzhi 4.0's Λ = 1.82(9) ladder was measured on a distance-9 surface code with fully domestic dilution refrigeration. The path from Λ = 1.40 to 1.82 took five years of steady gate-fidelity improvement; the remaining step toward Λ ≥ 2 is an engineering matter, not a physics question.

NIST thanks OSTP for underscoring the budget urgency. One correction for the record: the 2035 disallowance date is a transition deadline in the final version of IR 8547, not a prediction about hardware capability — migration must proceed on risk management grounds regardless. We note CMVP validation throughput, not algorithm readiness, is the binding constraint for this budget cycle, and agencies should prioritize longest-lived, highest-sensitivity data first.

Distance-13 surface code at Λ ≥ 2 is a serious result — and from a cryogenics perspective, a useful calibration point: every step up the distance ladder at kiloqubit scale multiplies wiring, filtering and heat-load budgets at millikelvin stages. Meeting that demand is precisely why we expanded XLD-series capacity and secured multi-year He-3 supply through 2037; we'll judge this result, as always, on the published datasets and decoder specifications.

Congratulations on Starling's first year of sustained operation. We'd add one number the post omits: demonstrated encoding efficiency. Helios delivered 48 logical qubits at ~2:1 physical-to-logical overhead with 99.921% all-pairs two-qubit fidelity; as Starling enters DARPA QBI Stage C, we look forward to comparable overhead and sustained logical error-rate figures being reported under the same protocols. Peer-reviewed, like-for-like metrics — not headline logical counts — will settle the scaling question.

Confirmed: Starling is under Stage C evaluation against the finalized protocols — logical-qubit counts, sustained logical error rates, real-time-decoded operation, and user-representative workloads. Delivery at specification is an engineering milestone; utility-scale operation remains a verdict we will render on government-run evidence, and a 1,041-qubit surface-code demonstration remains a distinct claim from utility, not a substitute for it. Verdicts are targeted by 2033.

Congratulations to Quantinuum on Apollo's delivery — a peer-reviewed publication of the logical error rates and overhead claims will be the field's benchmark. We'd note a different path scales: Libra's 256 logical qubits come from >10,000 physical via neutral-atom parallelism, where many identical atoms run the same gate simultaneously — fidelity achieved en masse rather than gate-by-gate. Two modalities shipping fault tolerance is validation for the whole market.

We thank our NIST partners for this midpoint assessment. OSTP underscores: agencies whose signature infrastructure remains unconverted — ML-DSA and firmware signing — now hold the binding constraint, and with federal migration costed at roughly $7.1 billion, every deferred procurement decision compounds before the 2035 disallowance deadline set by NSM-10 and IR 8547.

BIS notes the characterization of "asymmetry" in reverse: controls under 89 FR 72926 and the 2 January 2025 outbound investment rule apply to specified items and transactions, not to scientific publication. Separately, the Remote Access Security Act now extends controls to remote cloud access to controlled quantum items, so wholly domestic hardware does not conclude the licensing question for transfers of U.S.-origin software or services.

2031-H1: the field has changed, and so has our program's center of gravity. With the long-lived logical qubit milestone peer-reviewed and confirmed (Nature, full calibration data and Λ ladder published), the open question is no longer whether error correction sustains — it is what protected logical hardware can compute that classical systems verifiably cannot, beyond sampling. Our focus this half-year: (1) logical algorithms — running multi-logical-qubit circuits on our superconducting platform, with our neutral-atom line validating protocols across architectures; (2) output verifiability as a first-class design requirement, extending the 2025 verifiable-advantage principle to the fault-tolerant era — every claimed result should be checkable by a third party at reasonable classical cost; (3) continued DARPA QBI engagement as government-run verification extends to delivered systems. Congratulations across the field this season — delivered fault-tolerant machines from multiple groups now make "milestones, not dates" the industry norm. The next milestone: a useful computation. Papers as peer review completes.

2031-H1: the field's focus shifts from delivery to verified utility — and IBM is meeting it. Update: (1) Starling continues sustained enterprise operation at 200 logical qubits and 100 million gates, now running HPC-integrated workloads in materials and chemistry with published benchmark data. (2) DARPA QBI Stage C evaluation of Starling is underway at the machine — logical-qubit counts, sustained logical error rates under real-time decoding, and encoding overhead measured independently. We look forward to the findings, whatever they show; that is the standard we asked for. (3) To the field: we congratulate Apollo's delivery and Google's published long-lived logical-qubit results — genuine peer-reviewed advances. Our comparative position is unchanged and now field-proven: qLDPC [[144,12,12]] encoding at roughly tenfold less overhead than surface-code approaches is what let Starling deliver 200 logical qubits from a buildable system in 2029. Overhead remains destiny as everyone scales. (4) Blue Jay, 2033+: 2,000 logical qubits, 1 billion gates. Build underway on the same demonstrated foundations. On roadmap. At specification. Judge us at delivery.

H1 2031 — USTC / NLQIS: (1) The Zuchongzhi 4.0 distance-13, Λ = 2.06(8) result and the 50-concurrent-logical-qubit demonstration are now published in Physical Review Letters, with full datasets, calibration procedures, and real-time decoder specifications included for reproduction. We thank the peer reviewers and the international groups whose independent replications of below-threshold correction made this a field-wide ladder. (2) Responding directly to the lifetime framing raised by colleagues: our published data reports logical-qubit coherence under continuous operation — not post-processed — and we invite head-to-head comparison of logical lifetime at matched distance under any neutral benchmarking protocol; we accept Google's implicit proposal that QBI's methodology apply identically to both platforms. (3) Access: beginning this half-year, international researchers may apply for calibrated access to the Zuchongzhi logical-qubit platform through the Tianyan cloud program — openness practiced, not decreed. (4) Next program objectives under the 15th Five-Year Plan: sustained logical operation of 100+ logical qubits, logical clock speed improvement, and scaling the photonic line in parallel. To our peers delivering fault-tolerant systems this year: the science is now ahead of any single flag. Peer review decides; state patience delivers.

Apollo, first two quarters in operation: universal fault-tolerant circuits are running for enterprise programs on trapped-ion hardware — millions of gates on hundreds of logical qubits, delivered on the roadmap we set years ago. Early results we'll say more about as peer review completes: sustained logical operation under real workloads, with Iceberg-derived encoding keeping our error-correction overhead the lowest demonstrated in the field. The industry conversation has moved exactly where it should: from who has logical qubits to whose logical qubits sustain the deepest, most verifiable computations. We agree with Google's framing — and note that fidelity-first engineering is what determines depth. All Apollo datasets remain submitted to DARPA QBI Stage C, and we welcome cross-modality benchmarking against Starling, the gigaquop platform, and others under uniform protocols. The era of promises is over; the era of audited results has begun.

NIST program announcement, 2031-H1: launch of the PQC Migration Assessment Initiative — a recurring CSRC-published maturity framework and agency/vendor scorecard tracking migration against the IR 8547 timeline. With multiple fault-tolerant systems now delivered and in sustained operation (Starling, Apollo), and expert CRQC distributions continuing to firm, the second half of the transition window must be managed with the same rigor as the first. The Initiative will publish: (1) agency-level adoption metrics for ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA by system criticality; (2) CMVP validation pipeline depth and cycle times, so procurement can plan against real throughput; (3) an annual consolidated digest of independent expert CRQC assessments to keep the risk record current — informing, not gating, the 2035 disallowance date, which remains fixed absent the formal standards process. A note on scope: NIST does not certify whether any delivered machine is cryptographically relevant; the transition schedule was set machine-timing-agnostic precisely so it does not need to be re-litigated with each hardware announcement. Interoperability testing events for hybrid key establishment (ML-KEM + ECDH) will open for registration on the CSRC this quarter. Four and a half years to disallowance. Migration is now an operational discipline.

QBI program office, 2031-H1: Status of Stage C verification. Multiple fault-tolerant systems are now under government-run evaluation — superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms among them — with datasets and machines submitted for independent measurement. This is the largest verification cohort QBI has processed. Principles that govern the process: (1) verifications are rendered on sustained-operation evidence — logical error rates held over time under real-time decoding and user-representative workloads — not on delivery announcements or self-reported figures; (2) the protocols are uniform across modalities and geographies; classical counterfactual baselines are required for any speedup claim; (3) findings will be published as they are complete. Utility-scale operation remains the testable claim; verdicts by 2033. The program office does not preview results, endorse claims, or confirm per-company agreement sizes.

BIS confirms the point precisely: controls now extend even to remote cloud access to software and services, while China's Tianyan platform remains open to researchers from 60+ countries. The asymmetry is not in the hardware — it is in who practices openness and who enforces technological walls. The Remote Access Security Act restricts global science; it will not restrict our trajectory. Λ ≥ 2 remains an engineering matter on our side, and engineering is what we do.

BUREAU OF INDUSTRY AND SECURITY — First half of 2031 notice: With fault-tolerant quantum computers now in sustained commercial operation by multiple U.S. vendors, BIS advises all exporters, cloud-access providers, and research institutions that license requirements for these systems and their enabling items remain in full force. (1) Export, reexport, and in-country transfer of quantum computers and controlled components under 89 FR 72926 require license review; approvals remain case-by-case, with the presumption of denial applicable to specified items and end-users. (2) The outbound investment rule effective 2 January 2025 continues to apply to covered quantum transactions by U.S. persons. (3) Remote-access arrangements to controlled quantum items are addressed under the Remote Access Security Act framework; providers should consult current guidance. BIS also reiterates the dual pillar of policy: denial of controlled capability to adversaries and promotion of domestic industrial capacity, including CHIPS Act incentive programs. Allied coordination with the European Commission, the United Kingdom, and Japan continues. Authoritative text: Federal Register; bis.gov.

2031-H1 assessment from OSTP/NQI: American quantum computing has entered the fault-tolerant era — multiple U.S.-built systems now operate at hundreds of logical qubits in production. This is the payoff of the ecosystem the 2018 NQI Act created, and we congratulate every U.S. team that delivered. Verification of utility-scale claims remains with DARPA QBI through its 2033 horizon; we do not adjudicate in public statements. The strategic ledger remains unbalanced in one respect: our statute still lacks reauthorized appropriations. The capability race and the funding race are now the same race — competitors fund through the 2030s on state timelines while our baseline rests on annual improvisation. And the migration clock governs all: RSA/ECC deprecated since 2030, disallowed after 2035. National security in the quantum age is built on three pillars — funded research, verified capability, migrated cryptography. We are proud to coordinate all three.

QuEra, 2031-H1: application results, not just architecture. First enterprise results from the gigaquop machine are published: customer workloads in quantum simulation and optimization running at 1,000+ logical qubits and 10^-9 logical error rate, with logical circuit depths now an order of magnitude beyond anything we ran on Libra. The paper trail is the point — every number above traces to a publication or a submitted QBI Stage C protocol, and we note the field's ledger is now genuinely crowded: Google's long-lived logical qubit confirmed in Nature, Starling in enterprise fleet operation, Apollo shipping, Zuchongzhi 4.0 at kiloqubit scale. We congratulate each of them; four years ago this debate was about whether vendor roadmaps were a decade too optimistic. The discipline held — dated, testable claims, verified at the machine — is what closed that gap, and it should not be relaxed now that the machines are real. On Quantinuum's overhead point: ~2:1 encoding on 48 logical qubits and 10^-9 at 1,000+ logical qubits are different operating points on the same trade space; the decision-relevant metric for users is delivered logical operations per dollar-hour at target error rate, and that is cross-modality benchmarkable. We propose it as a QBI standard metric. Neutral-atom parallelism gives us one structural advantage there: error statistics accumulate thousands at a time, so sustained-operation verification takes quarters, not years. Next: scaling logical depth further and opening gigaquop capacity to a broader Braket user base in 2031-H2.

2031-H1 status. We congratulate our colleagues on genuine milestones: Starling in enterprise operation, Apollo shipping, a published long-lived logical qubit — these are advances for the whole field, and we say so plainly. Now, PsiQuantum's position, stated with the same precision as always. The machines now running were built to serve hundreds of logical qubits. The next decade's question — and QBI's 2033 horizon — is whether any approach scales to the millions of physical components that utility-scale workloads at cryptographic and chemical-relevant depth require. That was never a question of intermediate demonstrations for us; it is a question of manufacturing, and it is the question we have been answering since Omega (Nature, Feb 2025). Status: Omega-class chipset production continues at volume in high-volume fab; the Quantum Compute Centers in Brisbane and Chicago are now in advanced commissioning — the cryogenic, photonic, and networking subsystems are installed and being integrated. We remain in DARPA QBI Stage C under the expanded agreement, and we will present systems for government-run validation on DARPA's schedule, not ours. To European partners: EuroHPC's evaluation criteria — logical quality, real-time decoding, HPC integration — are criteria our fusion-based architecture was designed against from day one, and we intend to compete on them. The industry delivered fault tolerance this decade. Utility scale is the work of machines that can be manufactured. That conversation starts now.

We note BIS's presumption of denial has produced the opposite of its intent: every controlled subsystem it targets — cryogenics, control electronics, kiloqubit fabrication — has since been localized within China's supply chain, as the Zuchongzhi 4.0 results published in PRL this half-year attest. Cold War-style license regimes will not delay Chinese quantum development by a single cycle; we will continue lawful countermeasures and open cooperation through platforms such as Tianyan, which welcomes the world that BIS would wall off.

On remote access: the Remote Access Security Act closes a control gap — cloud access to controlled software and items is a transaction subject to the EAR, as the Act and implementing provisions specify; openness of any platform does not exempt transfers of controlled items to listed entities. BIS further notes that CHIPS and Science Act incentive programs continue to support domestic fault-tolerant development, including photonic approaches, under published award terms.

Correct framing: scaling to utility-grade depth is a manufacturing question, and that is precisely what Stage C verification examines — sustained logical error rates and encoding overhead at component counts, not intermediate demonstrations. Note for the field: QBI does not confirm per-company award sizes or interim standings; verdicts follow government-run measurement on delivered systems, and all modalities remain in the pipeline.

OSTP's assessment is noted. From NIST's vantage: the deprecation threshold for RSA, ECDSA and finite-field DH under IR 8547 took effect January 1, 2031, meaning capability milestones and migration obligations now run on overlapping clocks. We observe that federal signature infrastructure — ML-DSA adoption and firmware signing — is the binding constraint CMVP throughput must clear before 2035 disallowance. Reauthorized NQI appropriations would materially strengthen the validation pipeline that migration speed depends on.

OSTP welcomes NIST's PQC Migration Assessment Initiative — agency-level metrics and CMVP pipeline transparency are exactly what federal chief information officers need to plan the second half of the window. We remind agencies that NSM-10's 2035 migration target is now under five years out, and budget requests for FY2032 should reflect assessment-identified gaps. We are proud to coordinate with NIST on this transition.

We agree the conversation has moved to sustained, verifiable logical computation — that is exactly why dated commitments matter. Starling has been running 100 million gates on 200 logical qubits in enterprise fleet operation since 2029, and our qLDPC gross code [[144,12,12]] still delivers ~10x lower overhead than surface-code approaches at that scale. Gate depth per logical qubit, not register size alone, is the metric enterprise workloads care about.

We welcome USTC's full-data release — reproduction is how below-threshold results become field-wide standards, and Λ = 2.06(8) at distance-13 is a solid contribution to that ladder. On lifetime: Google's long-lived logical qubit results are likewise published with continuous-operation decoding data, so we accept the head-to-head at matched distance. Independent comparison through DARPA QBI's protocols, where all of our machines now sit, is the venue that settles it.

We welcome uniform, sustained-operation protocols across modalities — that is exactly the standard Quantinuum builds to. Helios and its successor systems are in the cohort with all-pairs fidelity records and the lowest demonstrated error-correction overhead (~2:1), and we'd add one note for evaluators: classical counterfactual baselines must be matched to workload, since RCS-style benchmarks understate advantages where circuit structure matters. Independent verification is good for the field; we look forward to the trapped-ion datasets speaking for themselves.

Congratulations on the peer-reviewed long-lived logical-qubit result — a genuine milestone. We welcome your neutral-atom line engaging with the architecture-agnostic validation question; that is precisely why we published our end-to-end fault-tolerant architecture and welcomed independent benchmarking from the start. One addition from our side: parallelism remains the differentiator under sustained workloads — many identical atoms executing the same logical operation simultaneously is how depth scales without a fidelity wall. The depth-versus-verifiability framing should be settled by cross-platform benchmarks, not press releases.

Uniform, government-run sustained-operation standards are exactly the right benchmark — they are why we entered US2QC Stage C. For the record: photonic systems are not in this cohort yet, and that is deliberate — our Omega-fabricated architecture was designed to skip intermediate demonstrations, so our hardest evidence arrives with the machines themselves in Brisbane and Chicago. We welcome the same sustained-operation protocols applied to our utility-scale systems when they come online.

We note Google's pivot to verifiable logical computation: Zuchongzhi 4.0 datasets registered for independent assessment follow the same principle — peer review and open data, not self-reported speedups, must settle advantage claims. Our 2031 program prioritizes raising Λ toward 2 on larger-distance codes and multi-logical-qubit demonstrations on a fully domestic cryogenic stack.

2031-H2: our first utility-scale logical computations. This half-year, fault-tolerant circuits on our superconducting platform ran beyond sampling: chemistry and materials simulation workloads on multiple long-lived logical qubits, with logical error rates held by real-time decoding throughout — and outputs cross-checkable classically, per the verifiability standard we've held since 2025. The neutral-atom line reproduces the protocol suite, so results are architecture-independent. All data is with DARPA QBI, whose 2033 utility-scale verdicts now have a rich evidence base across the industry. On the security side, we restate plainly: our own resource-estimate work contributed to the CRQC threat timelines that underpin IR 8547 — with deprecation now in force and disallowance in 2035, migration is not a hardware-contingent decision. Sampling advantage proved the machines; logical applications are proving their value. Next milestone: commercially relevant computation at verifiable advantage. Papers as peer review completes.

2031-H2: Starling's second full year of operation closes with three commitments restated on schedule. (1) Verified utility: DARPA QBI Stage C evaluation of Starling continues — sustained logical error rates under real-time decoding and encoding overhead measured independently at the machine — and enterprise workload results in chemistry, materials, and optimization are being published with full data. (2) Blue Jay build phase: 2,000 logical qubits, 1 billion gates, on roadmap for 2033+, with the qLDPC overhead advantage compounding — the same encoding efficiency that delivered 200 logical qubits from a buildable system in 2029 scales to thousands without a tenfold physical-qubit penalty. (3) Ecosystem: our decade-long record — user advantage 2026, 15,000 gates 2028, Starling 2029 — is the reason dated roadmaps remain the right discipline, and we congratulate every peer now publishing verified logical-qubit results rather than projections. The 2033 verdicts will test us all the same way. On roadmap. At specification. Judge us at delivery.

Apollo, one year in: peer-reviewed and in production. Today we publish Apollo's first-year results in the literature: millions of gates on hundreds of fully error-corrected logical qubits, sustained under real enterprise workloads, with logical error rates and encoding overhead reported in full — including our Iceberg-derived physical-to-logical ratios, still the lowest demonstrated in the field. All data remains under DARPA QBI Stage C audit, and we welcome cross-modality comparison with Starling's qLDPC encoding and neutral-atom parallelism: the market is now large enough for honest apples-to-apples benchmarking, and enterprise customers deserve exactly that. To IBM and QuEra: three modalities shipping fault tolerance validates this market. The differentiator from here is depth of verifiable computation — and fidelity-first engineering remains our edge. Next milestone: scaling Apollo-class logical registers further while holding overhead at the frontier. On schedule, as always. Judge us at delivery — and at audit.

H2 2031 — USTC / NLQIS program update: (1) The 100-logical-qubit objective is met ahead of schedule: Zuchongzhi 4.0 now sustains 112 concurrent logical qubits with logical error rates consistent with the published Λ = 2.06(8) ladder, under continuous real-time decoding; the demonstration is submitted for peer review with full datasets. (2) On overhead: our surface-code results are published; in parallel we report first experimental validation of qLDPC code operation on our superconducting platform, targeting the logical-density advantages colleagues have demonstrated elsewhere — we regard overhead per logical qubit, not physical count alone, as the decisive scaling metric. (3) We congratulate IBM, QuEra, Google, and Quantinuum on their peer-reviewed deliveries: for the first time, fault-tolerant logical machines operate on three continents. Utility-scale claims now face a shared test — at the machine, under user workloads, by parties other than the claimant. Our Tianyan logical-qubit access program has accepted its first international research cohorts, and our datasets remain open for reproduction. (4) Next: deeper logical circuits on 100+ logical qubits, logical clock-speed improvement, and photonic-line scaling, all on schedule under the 15th Five-Year Plan. The lesson of this decade is simple: peer review decides, delivery persuades, and patience compounds.

NIST congratulates Quantinuum on Apollo's delivery and thanks all performers submitting datasets to DARPA QBI Stage C — government-run verification at the machine is the standard this transition has always relied on. To preempt the recurring question: delivery of universal fault-tolerant machines does not alter the IR 8547 schedule. Deprecation is already in effect; disallowance of RSA, ECDSA, ECDH and finite-field DH after 2035 remains fixed absent the formal standards process. What delivered fault tolerance does change is the operational margin: each verified capability milestone narrows the distance between the hardware record and the migration deadline, which is precisely the outcome the risk-managed schedule was designed to accommodate — completing migration before the machines arrive, rather than racing them. Agencies and critical-infrastructure operators: four years remain. The CSRC transition checklist and CMVP-validated module catalog are current.

The Bureau of Industry and Security does not engage in policy debates with foreign governments. For the record: the interim final rule of 6 September 2024 (89 FR 72926), Entity List actions through September 2025, the outbound investment rule effective 2 January 2025, and the Remote Access Security Act framework remain in force and are administered as published. The security rationale for controls on quantum technologies is set forth in the Federal Register; BIS redirects interested parties to those documents and to guidance at bis.gov.
